items.body: Look at all those people! Everything seems bigger on Hour‘s newest album. There are fourteen people in the ensemble (four missing the photo shoot). The Bandcamp description is a thousand words long. The album is offered on black vinyl, colored vinyl, deluxe CD and promo CD. So why does Ghost Bridge sound so much smaller and more intimate ~ even more so than Subminiature? The answers are the arrangements and the brevity. On Ghost Bridge, the Philly ensemble led by Michael Cormier-O’Leary continues its slow shift from post-rock to modern composition. The pieces – and by extension, the instruments – are given more room to breathe. A half dozen tracks unfold in a concise 36 minutes. Late in the set, a vocal selection slows the pace to a pleasant crawl. Hour is still more Rachel’s than Low, but is carving out a niche at a pace similar to that of a stream cutting channels in stone. The title is taken from an “unrealized movie concept” about a disappearing and reappearing bridge. From this prompt, the album muses on tragedies, ghosts and the nature of the soul. Over a quarter of the album is devoted to the title track, whose very length suggests it bears the specter of post-rock. Solo piano is joined by light drums, then vibraphone, then all the other instruments in time, gathering like a crowd at a wake, forming layers of consolation, adding confidence and strength until the grief itself becomes a ghost. The end is a soft mist of notes, a few stragglers staying behind to whisper to the piano before they all go home. But where did it all begin? “Pearls” is the opening track, proceeding from a series of repeated notes to engage in happy permutations. Little sorrow can be intuited here; instead the starting point is a breezy, carefree day, filled with horse-drawn carriages and hot air balloons until the full stop at the three-minute mark, when darker clouds can be seen on the horizon: not yet here, but on their way. The pianist stumbles; the string players look up; the concentration of the percussionist is disrupted. The flautist resets the mood: the sorrow has not yet approached, so let us savor the now. The sedate ending sets up “Centralia,” a series of layered phrases that circle back and repeat like recurring thoughts or the motivational sentences of friends. Only after “Ghost Bridge” does “Sky Is Blue” emerge, perfectly placed as the first track on Side B, albeit jarring in the digital and CD versions. The lyrics, sung by Heeyoon Won, reveal it to be an extensive message from the great beyond, delivered by a loved one who is completely okay, filled with perspective, encouragement and hope. Should one not own the LP, we recommend moving “Sky Is Blue” to the finale. Given this sequencing, “So Long Without a Word” slips into the void at the end of “Ghost Bridge,” its melodic tones speaking directly to the soul, the full stop now at 2:00, followed by increasing energy and resolve. A third phase begins two minutes later with insistent, cinematic strums, then a playful series of shifts, jazz to chamber and back, like a playground ball. “Sonny” returns the timbre to post-rock and the mood to reflective yet ebullient, the ghost bridge now reappearing, the path between heaven and earth secure. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Watch an exclusive premiere of the film of Ava Rasti’s The River, first performed as part of the 2025 Semibreve festival. The River by Iranian-born Berlin-based composer Ava Rasti was commissioned by Portuguese festival Semibreve and first presented on 25 October 2025 at the Capela Imaculada do Seminário Menor in Braga. The performance brought together Rasti and a string quartet composed of Filipa Abreu (violin), Vânia Oliveira (viola), Tiago Mendes (cello) and Catarina Coelho (cello). The work takes the Piave river in northern Italy as its inspiration, a landscape in which the present is intertwined with the traces of wars and violence from its past. Rasti constructs these fragmented memories, recontextualised and transformed into sounds. Wire subscribers can read Claire Sawer's review of Semibreve 2025 here.

items.album: [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal)
items.excerpt: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim M
items.body: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim Martin has been Maps and Diagrams since the early 2000s, and the entry point for a lot of people into his catalog is Polytuft-Tech, released in 2003 on Expanding Records, an album that got filed under IDM, ambient, and glitch at a moment when those three words together still meant something specific and rigorous. That record ran on clicky drums that whirred like clockwork under warm, streamlined melodies. It landed near the tail end of IDM’s most experimentally saturated period, right as the genre itself was quietly transitioning into whatever came next, and it stands as one of the more melodically generous statements from that stretch. Both returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) are nowhere near that record sonically. Drums are gone almost entirely. Glitch has been replaced by drift. But it’s still unmistakably Tim, the same restrained, resonant signature that’s followed him through two decades of output, just aged into something quieter. Both albums arrive within weeks of each other on different labels with different histories attached. returning light is Home Normal‘s second release from Tim this year, following tone isolation, his actual debut on the label despite Home Normal running for over seventeen years, a gap explained by the fact that Tim‘s earliest UK work went through Nomadic Kids Republic, Home Normal‘s sister label, back in 2011 with Lights Will Call On You and The Town Beneath The Sea. beneath still stars comes out on handstitched*, the label Tim runs himself, which has carried his more private and experimental output for years alongside releases like In Circles. One album through someone else’s curatorial lens, one through his own. That distinction matters more than it initially seems to. Ambient releases should never get judged track by track in isolation. The genre works as a collective experience, an album like this either builds a sustained emotional environment across its runtime or it doesn’t, and no individual piece can really save or sink that outcome on its own. What matters more is whether the melodies that surface actually resonate, whether they invoke something specific rather than just occupying space. Both of these records succeed at that, though they do it through slightly different means. “ArcWorld-6.4 Rev.42 [sgl.break]” from beneath still stars is one of the more fascinating pieces across either release, another example of the part A / part B structure that’s shown up in other reviews recently. It connects two ideas without part B ever feeling like a continuation of part A. Instead it functions as an introduction to something entirely different, and the transition is peaceful in a way that most of this album is. The track titles throughout beneath still stars read almost like technical drafts, numbered revisions, hertz values, file extensions in brackets like [static] or [lost.wav] or [mem.void]. That naming isn’t arbitrary. It reads like an iteration system, drafts selected and refined specifically rather than titled decoratively after the fact. “Raddius.ocean-IX [r.36-04hz]” is another two-part piece, but this one connects rather than diverges, a drone-like melodic note giving way to a dreamlike synth tuned to a specific frequency, which the title tells you outright. Intentional down to the hertz. “beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels.” ~J. Batista A different level of drone entirely :: returning light sits in the same emotional register but sounds noticeably different sonically. There are small clicks and glitches scattered through certain tracks, and the pads and atmospheres carry a different weight than what’s happening on beneath still stars. “falling rainbows” uses static hits inside its pad environments to create reverbed textures that read almost like snare hits, except Tim‘s building that rhythmic tension entirely out of pad effects and reverb rather than anything resembling a drum sample. “just moving” introduces keys that sound almost like distortion at first before resolving into something prettier the longer you sit with it, a different level of drone entirely, since nothing here holds on a single note. There’s room for other melodies to form and enter, and they do. “somewhat virtual interactions” is a favorite, what sounds like a distorted “ahhh” vocal fragment sits so subtly in the mix that it changes the character of the pads around it, and there are field recording glitches scattered throughout that open up real space inside the track. “Open Water” plays almost like an audio representation of a shishi-odoshi—that traditional Japanese bamboo water fountain that fills, tips, empties, and resets in a slow repeating cycle. Tim‘s using effects here the same way that device uses gravity and water, building a soft, cyclical sense of rhythm entirely out of texture rather than percussion. “ouvertures” closes the album starting soft and distorted, and around the 3:55 mark a low humming frequency starts creeping in that sounds baked into the synth itself, eventually rolling and degrading the audio as the track winds down. A genuinely cool effect to end on. “Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter.” ~J. Batista There’s a version of this review that picks a favorite between the two records. That version would be missing the point entirely. beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels. beneath still stars is the more clinical of the pair. Drafted, revised, numbered like lab notes, every track title reading like a version history for a synth that never stops evolving. Twenty years removed from Polytuft-Tech‘s clockwork drums and whirring percussion, Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter. These two records don’t argue for themselves. They don’t need to. They just sit there, patiently, until you notice forty minutes have passed and you’ve barely moved. Home Normal got the warmer half. handstitched*—Tim‘s own label, his own house, got the rawer, more exacting one. He gets to have it both ways. So does anyone who sits with both records long enough to stop telling them apart. beneath still stars is available on handstitched* and returing light is available on Home Normal. beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagramsThe post [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — Truly mind blowing album. Arguably one of the most manifold records from the dusk of that decade. HIGH TIDE have been one of the most important underground rock acts of that era. This album really blew my mind the first time I heard it. I almost did not believe that it released in 1969. Very few bands were so heavy back then. HIGH TIDE is so damn heavy, it really pisses me off that I can't recall a single magazine or online "list" of proto-metal bands that mentions these guys. You can find fragments of early doom in songs like "Futilist's lament" & "Missing out". You can hear neoclassical influences on the guitar riff on "Walking down their outlook". Also, on the same song, listen carefully the guitar lick on 2:20 (Judas Priest anyone?!?!?). And that violin... Majestic. Enchanting. Listen to "Pushed, but not forgotten". Amazing stuff, honestly. Some people may say that the [&*!#]ty production fits with the music and the atmosphere, I say it steals the music's grandeur.

items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comA third exquisite offering. The talented Italian quartet Aether is back with an incredibly solid, mature, refined, and creative album, one that fans of jazz fusion, progressive rock, and music that appeals to the senses will enjoy from beginning to end. Across 43 minutes and six tracks, the musicians treat us to a series of sonic landscapes that range from relaxing to frenetic, from atmospheric to deeply sensory, moving seamlessly between rock, post-rock, ambient, and classical music. It all begins with "Oort Cloud," whose opening seconds are atmospheric and otherworldly, creating a contemplative, dark mood. Little by little, new elements and sounds emerge, making you feel as though you are floating through space, caught somewhere between uncertainty and curiosity, until everything erupts at the 2:30 mark and a new rhythm takes over, retaining that dark sound that at times reminds me of early-70s King Crimson. As the minutes go by, the band introduces more colors, with the keyboards becoming a crucial element. Nevertheless, the atmospheres created by the bass, guitar, and drums come together to form a truly fascinating sonic experience. Next comes "Vogon," where the bass maintains a steady pulse while the guitar, keyboards, and drums appear here and there, gradually moving from uncertainty toward a sense of resolution as a distinctly jazzy melody begins to take shape. The very distinctive voice of the theatrical Claudio Milano emerges to recite a poem, creating one of the album's most unique moments. Shortly after his voice fades away, the music explodes, and jazz gives way to rock, with Andrea Ferrari's guitar charging forward like a whirlwind of emotions, compelling you to move and simply enjoy the music. The sonic landscapes shift in fascinating ways on "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres." It begins by creating spacious, otherworldly soundscapes that, after two and a half minutes, take on an almost psychedelic essence, thanks first to the hypnotic bass of Andrea Grumelli, who guides the way as the guitar, synths, and drums deliver a daring and wonderful blend of space rock and jazz. This is one of my favorite tracks on the album. "La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince" features Andrea Serino's piano as the central element and guiding force of this literary-inspired passage. Beyond the blend of jazz and classical music brought to life by the piano, I love the fretless bass and its wonderfully fluid, graceful notes. I am also particularly fond of the deliciously sensory percussion Matteo Ravelli plays at the beginning, which he later contrasts with his electronic devices. Another majestic moment arrives with "Panta Rei." Its eight minutes unleash the quartet's imagination and creativity, showing us that after three studio albums, these musicians understand one another exceptionally well and flow together naturally, not only as accomplished instrumentalists but, more importantly, as a band. And although there are several darker, denser moments, I love the balance they achieve, as we suddenly find ourselves immersed in passages that feel bright and full of promise. At one point, they even reminded me of Focus. And yes, progressive rock is very much present here. Finally, the album reaches its brilliant conclusion with "Swerve." Over the course of its ten minutes, Aether delivers the climax of the entire work, a clear testament to the evolution of their sound and their boundless creativity. The band brings together a rich mix of genres and emotions, allowing listeners to immerse themselves in progressive passages, profound atmospheres, and enveloping, emotionally charged textures. The rhythm and intensity gradually build from the halfway point onward, creating a sonic spectrum that makes you want to move with the music, feel it, savor every moment, and truly make it your own. Congratulations to Aether on such a solid release. I absolutely loved it.

items.body: Review by Logan — Looking Beyond The Beautiful Space Out in the CountryThe short-form record tends to work on a different logic than a full LP. I value EPs that carry their own weight as intentional, self-contained pieces rather than just acting as a way to repackage existing music for sale.Much like a short film, an EP can use its brevity to settle into a specific mood or texture, without needing to extend those ideas across the length of a full studio album.Godspeed You Black Emperor!'s Slow Riot for New Zero Kanada does this well, letting tracks like "Moya" and "BBF3" create a heavy and distinct presence in under thirty minutes. Boards of Canada seems to approach the format similarly. A record like In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country does not feel like leftover tracks -- it works as an independent soundscape where the brief runtime is used for deliberate atmosphere.An important aspect of In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country is that these tracks do not appear on other major releases, which makes the EP an essential piece of their discography rather than a minor supplement. It stands out as one of my very favourite EPs. Listening to it highlights a beautiful and mysterious ambient density built on a sort of melancholy, discomforting and comforting nostalgia.I especially adore the tracks "Kid for Today" and "In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country" but I think the whole record is superb taken as a whole. "Zoetrope" did not at first appeal much, but during consecutive listens I got how its minimalist ambience worked with and added to the rest of the release. It helps to demonstrate how their use of repetitive, cyclical structures can reveal deeper qualities when one sits with the textures over a period of time. That highlights to me how a track can reward patience.I give it 5 stars as one of my most essential EPs.

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — One of my favorite albums of 1969 hands down. So many styles of music one can find here. Blues, psychedelia, jazz, classical, rock. All of them combined to provide a sample of proto-prog in the late 60s British scene. Songs like "Isadora", "Waterways", "Bathers", "Moth" are majestic. Geoff Nicholson delivers some really beautiful and heart-warming vocal harmonies. But, Dave Arbus steals the show here. With his electric violin and his flute, he blesses our ears with some enchanting melodies. This album really could be close to perfect, if it weren't for those free jazz/improvisations on the songs "Centaur woman" & "In the stable of the Sphinx" which in my opinion kind of mess up a little bit the whole atmosphere of the album.Nevertheless, this is a really strong album, that the fans of the early prog rock era should check out.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — When I first heard a few tracks by this Finnish band, I gradually realized that what captivated me was the blend of King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's irreverence toward musical genres, an approach that, while experimenting with them all, still respects them and follows their rules. I was also reminded of The Cardigans: a mix of tradition and the past, combined with a freshness where technology, jazz, and a unique brand of pop came together. Their debut album opens on a serious note with classical piano and violins, key elements of their sound, and the magical voice of Eeva Rajakangas; on the track "T�nne saakka ei aurinko paista," she recites the lyrics, creating a powerful and truly special moment. Kadenssi reveals the strong influence of Nordic traditional music, austere, profound, and almost sacred, and Celtic music, danceable and luminous, sharing a common thread in that both border on the mystical.With the fourth track, Kahdeksas p�iv�, rock and modernity enter the mix, while maintaining that distinctive nine-piece lineup, featuring two violins and a saxophone, where the true fusion begins. A folk atmosphere, driven by the flute, occasionally evokes the folk-rock sound of Jethro Tull; yet, modern drum loops and Eeva's spoken-word vocals merge into a blend of jazz, funk, and punk. Add to this a dissonant chorus and a distorted, psychedelic cabaret vibe, and it feels as though we are witnessing a whole new album within the album itself."Planeetta" plays with space and silence; Eeva's voice sings and then recedes, as does the piano, eventually revealing a jazz-infused atmosphere driven by violins and saxophone, lending the track a distinctive character. It then returns to Celtic roots, yet approaches them not in the traditional manner, but with a rock and funk sensibility, featuring a syncopated, irregular rhythm."08" continues with the distinctly postmodern vibe created by Eeva's spoken vocals, almost prophetic in tone, which has become a signature, recognizable style for the band. Just as Pessi Jouste's classical training is evident in the violin work, Aino Kallio's influence shines through on the piano; at times, the music evokes the atmosphere of chamber music, at others, Eastern and jazz styles reminiscent of Hiromi Uehara, or even the experimental approach of Alain Rochette (from the band Present). When the sound grows heavier, it becomes dense and dark, yet the strings and Eeva Rajakangas are always there, ensuring we never quite plunge over the precipice."Tarina" ventures into new territory; while Eeva sings and phrases with great freedom, she does so in tandem with a band that evokes the anarchic melodies of the Lounge Lizards, until the violins launch into a sort of tango reminiscent of the track "Palmiers En Pots" by the Belgian group Aksak Maboul. It is not even far-fetched to draw parallels with the Rock in Opposition scene; one can even detect traces of the early, defiant Bj�rk, alongside the bass-clarinet blues of Jaakko Arola."Vesi" evokes a violin-infused cabaret sung by Ute Lemper, yet the arrangements steer the sound toward danceable rhythms infused with punk currents, waves that surge in and recede. The band adapts perfectly to this variety of styles, skillfully navigating the challenge of maintaining overall cohesion. They stand as an impenetrable, unbreakable shield, much like the Baltic Shield, reflecting that Nordic light which lasts for months; a duration that pales in comparison to the enduring scope of their musical and artistic vision.

items.body: Anyankofo means friends in Fante, and the Danish seven-piece Total Hip Replacement have been collecting them in Ghana since a mini-tour there in 2013. In the winter of 2021 they formed a nine-piece band in Accra with Ghanaian highlife, reggae and gospel musicians and gave it that name, which also titles the album the group recorded at Kwame Yeboah‘s Kwashibu studio, released in 2022. A later trip to Ghana took them to Kumasi, the Ashanti capital and one of highlife’s strongholds, and a week of jamming there with players from Frafra gospel singer Florence Adooni‘s band and with Nsoroma of Accra highlife band Santrofi produced “The Search”. It is the latest single ahead of the album Ehum, and the band say it holds on to the improvised feel of the jams. The song is about hunting for purpose in a society that keeps speeding up, where the pressure to get ahead alone costs people their connection to each other. Singer and trombonist Victor West Hosbond fronts the band’s horn section, the signature of their sound, and on this single it rides a highlife rhythm. The band describe the mood they chased as “the hopeful spot between melancholy and euphoria“. They filmed the video over a couple of days at an old farmhouse in France during this summer’s tour, with Nell Le Corre behind the camera. Ehum, which the band translate as storm, comes out on 27 November with Ivorian reggae singer Tiken Jah Fakoly among the guests. A West African run through Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana opens the tour, then Danish dates follow from February into April, among them ALICE in Copenhagen on 26 February and Aarhus on 27 March. items.body: While the title of Sandrine Piau and David Kadouch’s new project translates to “tales,” the performers in their accompanying interview note the complexity of their theme: light and dark tales, they observe, follow us into adulthood, creating a multidimensional way to tell stories. Contes Amazon Presto Apple The offerings here are indeed diverse: Piau plays to her strengths in French art song but also extends her range to include songs by Wolf and Shostakovich. Jeanne Bernard’s Trois chansons de Bilitis opens the program; this set is not to be confused with Debussy’s more famous cycle. The songs themselves are based on entirely different poems from Pierre Louÿs’ collection, with Debussy choosing themes of sensual love and nature. Bernard, on the other hand, elects to depict scenes of childhood and innocence. It’s a shame that her version is so often overshadowed, as it is a delightful cycle. Piau’s vocal timbre and temperament fit beautifully, breathing much vitality into the songs. Les petits enfants (track 1) is effusive and imaginative, while Les contes (track 2) takes a gentler turn. Several times, the textures thin to a single line in each part, and the duo creates a beautiful tenderness in such moments. Reynaldo Hahn’s À Chloris (track 4) draws unmistakably upon Baroque styles. Piau’s familiarity with this repertoire through her extensive Baroque discography serves her well: her vocal control is not just meticulous but reveals an exquisite level of clarity. In some ways, I found that her voice takes on an almost flute- or recorder-like quality. Kadouch’s accompaniment possesses a similar pristine quality but also brings a sense of placid warmth. Wally Karveno’s La robe de lune (track 5) is a quirky waltz that vacillates between the lush and bold and the quiet and introspective. The performers capture the spirit of each character without losing the anticipation the text conveys. The ending, though, offers a moment of unexpected irony: the warmth the duo evokes at the arrival of the major key actually speaks to the saddest moment in the poem. La fille aux cheveux de lin (track 6) gives Kadouch a solo moment. Consistent with his duo playing, his style is uncontrived and speaks directly to the listener. However, parts of Debussy’s prelude could use a little more time to let the harmonies bloom or for the color changes to work their full magic. Maurice Ravel’s Cinq mélodies populaires grecques is a series of five vignettes of traditional Greek life and features some of the most vivacious and sensitive performances from the duo. The excitement of a wedding morning comes through Piau’s breathy phrases and Kadouch’s delicate chimes, vividly reminiscent of wedding bells in the distance. The words of Là-bas, vers l’église (track 8) may be relatively simple, but the performance says otherwise: Kadouch’s opening chords create a nuanced sparkle while Piau brings a new level of expanse and resonance to her lines. The folk element is alive and well in Quel galant m’est comparable (track 9) but without losing the refinement of Ravel’s musical style. Sandrine Piau and David Kadouch. Photo © Sandrine Expilly. Among the non-French repertoire, Hugo Wolf’s Die Geister am Mummelsee (track 13) from the Mörike-Lieder shows a different side of Piau’s vocal profile. Up to this point, her light coloratura range has featured prominently, but this song brings out a warmer, lyric quality. It holds up very well even over Kadouch’s thicker accompaniment, which also allows the pianist to unleash a fuller, more powerful sound we’ve not yet heard. One of the best selections on the album is Richard Strauss’ Wiegenlied (track 14), whose ebullience is captured in the piano part that mimics flowing water. Meanwhile, Piau assumes a presence that draws on both her strengths—high-register clarity and middle-register glow—to create a highly expressive narrative. Shostakovich’s Ophelia’s Song (track 26) is the album’s emotional low point, though it comes a little too late in the program. Still, it’s a welcome contrast to the lighter songs. The most striking difference from the other songs is the scoring for voice and cello. The poignancy of the string instrument brings an added level of desolation to the music. Piau once again turns to her lyric timbre here in an interpretation that is both soulful and devastating. Contes is yet another well-programmed and thoughtfully rendered album from Piau and her collaborators, and one that showcases her expressive versatility. Warmly recommended. Recommended Comparisons Ravel: Cinq mélodies populaires grecques Sabine Devieilhe, Alexandre Tharaud | Gerald Finley, Julius Drake | Mady Mesplé, Dalton Baldwin | Gérard Souzay, Dalton Baldwin The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: English post-punk band Killing Joke released their self-titled debut album, “Killing Joke,” on 5 October 1980 through E.G. Records, distributed by Polydor Records. The record turns 46 this year. Killing Joke recorded the album in August 1980 at Marquee Studios in London and produced it themselves, with Phil Harding as engineer. Drummer Paul Ferguson described the sessions as recorded live with “no overdubs to speak of.” The eight-track UK LP runs: “Requiem” “Wardance” “Tomorrow’s World” “Bloodsport” “The Wait” “Complications” “S.O.36” “Primitive” The original US pressing added “Change,” the B-side of the “Requiem” single, between “Complications” and “S.O.36.” “Wardance” came out as a single in February 1980, ahead of the album, and “Requiem” followed as a single in September 1980. The album entered the UK Albums Chart on 25 October 1980 at number 41 and later peaked at number 39. Its cover collages a photograph by Don McCullin of CS gas clashes in Derry, Northern Ireland, in 1971, designed by Mike Coles. In 2019, Pitchfork placed the album at number 9 on its list of the 33 best industrial albums of all time. “The Wait” was covered by Metallica on the 1987 “Garage Days Re-Revisited” EP and later included on “Garage Inc.,” “Primitive” was covered by Helmet in 1993, and “Requiem” was covered by Foo Fighters in 1997 as a B-side to “Everlong.” About Killing Joke Killing Joke formed in October 1978 in Notting Hill, London. Jaz Coleman (vocals, keyboards) and Paul Ferguson (drums) met in late 1978 and placed an announcement in Melody Maker in February 1979 reading “Bass, lead, to tell the killing joke, we mean it man!” Guitarist Geordie Walker and bassist Martin “Youth” Glover answered and completed the original line-up. The band released its debut EP, “Turn to Red,” as a 10-inch on 26 October 1979 on Malicious Damage, the label Killing Joke ran with graphic artist Mike Coles. Recorded in August 1979 at Gooseberry Sound in London, the EP drew airplay from BBC Radio 1’s John Peel. The “Almost Red” EP followed that November, and the single “Nervous System,” with “Turn to Red” as its B-side, came out in December 1979. Killing Joke then signed to E.G. Records for the self-titled debut album, released on 5 October 1980. The band’s next albums were “What’s THIS For…!” (1981) and “Revelations” (1982), after which Youth left the band and was replaced by Paul Raven on bass. “Fire Dances” followed in 1983 and “Night Time” in 1985, the album that carried the single “Love Like Blood” and brought the band its widest chart exposure to date. Killing Joke continued recording and touring into the 2010s with albums including “Absolute Dissent” (2010), “MMXII” (2012) and “Pylon” (2015), with Jaz Coleman and Geordie Walker as the group’s only constant members. Geordie Walker died in November 2023 at the age of 64, as Side-Line reported at the time. The band’s 1980 debut album remains the record that introduced the Killing Joke sound now marking its 46th anniversary this October.

items.body: Colossloth released a video for “Encoded Divinity” on 3 October 2026, a track from the album “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites.” The album came out 2 October 2026 on Cold Spring Records, the project’s sixth release for the label. The video was produced by HAONDOKU Productions. The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites by Colossloth Watch the video for ‘Encoded Divinity’ The video is available on YouTube: COLOSSLOTH – ‘Encoded Divinity’ Promo Video. “Encoded Divinity” opens the album and runs 5:08. ‘The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites’ tracklist The album was announced in September with its full tracklist: “Encoded Divinity” (5:08) “Calculate Your Revolution” (7:00) “Awaiting MENA” (9:04) “Undertow Atlas” (10:34) “Only Adrift” (8:00) Cold Spring describes the album as centered on Theta Noir, a collective built around worship of Mena, a fictional artificial intelligence deity. The label calls the record “an automaton chant of cybernetic worship.” The album is available on CD in a matt-laminate digipak (catalogue number CSR375CD) through Cold Spring’s webstore, and for download via Bandcamp. Colossloth played an album launch show at The Globe in Glossop on 3 October 2026, alongside T.A.G.C. (Adi Newton of Clock DVA), Satøri and Llyn Y Cwn. Further dates follow on 7 November at St Anne’s in Barnstaple with Satøri and A Waste of Damnation, and from 27 to 29 November at Sheffield General Cemetery’s In The Black Midwinter event with The Golden Age of Doing Nothing and Decommissioned Forests. About Colossloth Colossloth is the solo project of Leicester, UK musician Wooly Woolaston, active since 2008. Woolaston has described Colossloth as “a one man Experimental Electronic artist where there are no rules to recording or playing music,” with a sound that has moved from long guitar drones toward harsher electronics with sections of melody. Woolaston released Colossloth’s first album through Doom Structure in 2008, followed by releases on Doom Mantra Records in 2009 and Dark Meadow Recordings in 2011. He later signed to Cold Spring Records, releasing “Anchored By Lungs” (2014), “Outstretch Your Hand for the Impress of Truth” (2015), “Heathen Needles” (2017), “Plague Alone” (2020) and “Promethean Meat” (2022), the latter incorporating drum samples and harsher rhythmic elements. Colossloth also appeared on the label’s “Arise – A Cold Spring Sampler” compilation alongside Coil, Merzbow and Mz.412, among others. Colossloth’s fifth Cold Spring album, “The Harmony Knife,” followed on 28 February 2025, a concept record drawing on Ted Kaczynski’s “Industrial Society and Its Future” and its argument for the psychological necessity of struggle, known as “the power process.” “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites,” released 2 October 2026, is Colossloth’s sixth album for Cold Spring Records, now accompanied by a video for its opening track, “Encoded Divinity.”

items.body: Swedish duo Svaj. released a remix of the alan is waiting track “where you disappear” on 2 October 2026. The one-track single, titled “where you disappear (Svaj. Rebuild),” streams on Spotify and is available for download on Bandcamp and Subvert. The original song was written and sung by alan is waiting, the recording name of a Stockholm-based electronic artist whose debut album, “The Last of You,” came out in 2024. Svaj., the duo of Anders O Öhgren and Tomas Z Westberg based in Blackeberg, Stockholm, reworked the track for the remix. The release keeps alan is waiting’s original vocals. In a newsletter announcement, Svaj. described the result as “a wonky, New Order-tinged full-on synth-pop hit song.” where you disappear – Svaj. rebuild by Svaj., alan is waiting A visualizer for “where you disappear (Svaj. Rebuild)” is available on YouTube. About Svaj. Svaj. is the Stockholm duo of Anders O Öhgren and Tomas Z Westberg, based in the Blackeberg district of the city. The duo releases through its own TZW Produktion imprint. Svaj.’s Bandcamp profile describes its sound as “voice, electronics and bass. Minimal, experimental and industrial, yet melodic and danceable,” and compares it to Joy Division and Front 242. Svaj. issued its debut EP, “Rewind,” in March 2022. The songs reworked tracks originally recorded on tape in 1988, revisited with a Yamaha CS-10 synthesizer and a 1960s Tandberg reel-to-reel recorder. The duo’s second release, “Until We Fall,” followed in 2023. In 2024, Svaj. released the single “Cut Me Up,” a reworking of a song first written by Alien Waveform in 1989 and later issued as “Contagion” on the 1993 compilation “Tapping the Wires (A Selection of Futuristic Electro Mindbeats).” The digital single included a remix by UK industrial act Portion Control. The same year, Svaj. contributed “Brända Barn,” a reworking of a 1980 Swedish punk song, to the six-act compilation “SVÄRTA.” Svaj. released its third collection, “Maggots,” a six-track release, on 17 May 2025 through TZW Produktion on vinyl, CD and digital formats. The record includes a cover of John Cale’s 1974 track “Fear Is a Man’s Best Friend” and features contributions from Perra Wikström on contrabass and guitar and vocal effects from Devoid. Svaj. issued four music videos from “Maggots” through 2025, for “Experience,” “Fear,” “Portent” and, in October 2025, “Piglet.” The duo released the single “Patterns” on 19 February 2026. Svaj.’s catalog now runs from the 2022 “Rewind” EP through this month’s “where you disappear (Svaj. Rebuild)” remix.

items.body: Berlin-based darkwave act Night Nail released the single “Vile Train” on 2 October 2026 through Icy Cold Records. The track is the first digital single from the band’s forthcoming full-length album “Infinite Fountain,” set for release on 6 November 2026 through the same French label. A video for “Vile Train” accompanies the single. Night Nail’s Brandon Robert wrote “Vile Train” after a visit to the ash-covered ruins of Pompeii, Italy, where a Roman fresco depicting an angel and a demon locked in embrace became the song’s starting point. The lyrics follow two dreamers from separate realities who meet at the edge of their daydreams, fall into an obsession, and become trapped in a psychological cage of their own making. Robert describes the result as a “sonic assault of dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” “Vile Train” was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago and co-produced by Night Nail in Berlin, with additional vocals and guitar by VV & the Void, the darkwave project of Berlin musician Valentina Veil. Watch the video for ‘Vile Train’ The official video for “Vile Train” is available on YouTube: Night Nail – ‘Vile Train’ (Official Video). ‘Infinite Fountain’ due 6 November “Infinite Fountain” is available for presale on Bandcamp ahead of its 6 November 2026 release through Icy Cold Records. “Vile Train” streams on Spotify. Infinite Fountain by Night Nail About Night Nail Night Nail was founded in Los Angeles in 2013 by Brandon Robert and Justin Deaktiviere. Michael Carpenter Jr. on guitar, David Cluff on bass and Bryan Panzeri on drums joined for the project’s early releases. The project is now based in Berlin, Germany. An early self-titled EP drew press, college radio and blog coverage across the US, Europe, South America and Australia. The band’s debut album, “LA Demons,” was released in July 2018 on Cleopatra Records. Its title draws on Dostoevsky’s novel “Demons.” The sophomore album, “March to Autumn,” followed on 15 October 2020 through Cold Transmission Music. Pete Burns of Kill Shelter co-produced, mixed and mastered the record. Touring and session musicians Valentina Veil, Ilja Gavrilenko and Manuel Wagner contributed additional parts. In September 2023, Night Nail released the single “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher,” the first taste of the album “Fates Explained” on Metropolis Records. The single reached the top five of the Deutsche Alternative Charts. The “Fates Explained” video single followed that November. In January 2024, the band released a video for “Cracks In My Heart,” with Luna De La Torre on vocals, and in July 2024 issued “Early Demons & Demos,” a 10th-anniversary edition of early material. “Vile Train,” released 2 October 2026 through Icy Cold Records, is the first single from “Infinite Fountain,” due 6 November 2026.

items.body: Raveiac, a new rave-punk project from Turkey, released the compilation “Rave-Punk Rituals Vol. 1” on SoundCloud on 2 October 2026. The five-track set gathers “Backstall,” “Sweat & Slit,” “Rust & Strobe,” “Concrete Fever” and “Swallow the Noise,” tagged as techno on the platform. The compilation is part of a wider opening catalog. Raveiac released five tracks on 2 October: “Concrete Fever,” “Bite the Wire,” “Just One More,” “Swallow the Noise” and “I Feed It.” Two more, “Rust & Strobe” and “Sweat & Slit,” followed on 3 October, and “Backstall” closed the run on 4 October, for eight tracks in three days. There is no Bandcamp page yet. The catalog streams exclusively through Raveiac’s SoundCloud profile. Raveiac’s own description connects the project to “industrial rave, hard techno, breakbeat, EBM, gabber and digital hardcore,” through what it calls “a direct punk vocabulary: repeated commands, physical hooks and lyrics shaped by concrete rooms, surveillance, machinery, appetite and loss of control.” The project’s SoundCloud bio reads in full: “Rave-punk from Turkey. Dirty industrial raves, broken breaks, and digital decay. Repost what hits. Push it deeper underground.” ‘Rust & Strobe’ and ‘Swallow the Noise’ Raveiac singled out two tracks from the set for press attention. “Rust & Strobe” opens on metallic percussion and broken drums and closes on what the project calls “an acid-charged chorus.” “Swallow the Noise” is described as a faster industrial-rave track carried by a chanted vocal line and distorted production. Raveiac also presents a visual identity drawn from photocopied zines, neon imagery, torn paper, halftone noise and analog damage. About Raveiac Raveiac launched in October 2026 as an independent rave-punk project from Turkey. Between 2 and 4 October 2026, the project released eight tracks on SoundCloud: “Concrete Fever,” “Bite the Wire,” “Just One More,” “Swallow the Noise” and “I Feed It” on 2 October, “Rust & Strobe” and “Sweat & Slit” on 3 October, and “Backstall” on 4 October. Five of those tracks, “Backstall,” “Sweat & Slit,” “Rust & Strobe,” “Concrete Fever” and “Swallow the Noise,” make up the compilation “Rave-Punk Rituals Vol. 1”.

items.body: Einstürzende Neubauten’s debut studio album, “Kollaps,” turns 45 this year. The German industrial band released the record on 5 October 1981 through the Hamburg label ZickZack. It remains the first official full-length release by Blixa Bargeld, N.U. Unruh and F.M. Einheit under the Einstürzende Neubauten name. “Kollaps” runs 38 minutes across eleven tracks, recorded in Berlin in 1981 and produced by the band itself. The album mixes rough punk-derived song structures with noise generated from self-built devices, electronics and metal plates and other found objects, a method that became the band’s signature. The tracklist includes “Tanz Debil,” “Steh auf Berlin,” “Negativ Nein,” “U-Haft Muzak,” “Draußen ist Feindlich,” “Schmerzen Hören (Hören mit Schmerzen),” “Jet’M” (a cover of Serge Gainsbourg’s “Je t’aime… moi non plus”), the title track “Kollaps,” “Sehnsucht,” “Vorm Krieg” and “Hirnsäge.” Later CD reissues appended additional tracks, including a live 1987 recording of “Negativ Nein.” Trouser Press described the record as “one of the most shocking visions ever committed to vinyl.” “Kollaps” is also listed in the reference book “1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die.” The album has since been reissued, including a 2002 edition paired with the 1982 dub companion “Stahldubversions.” About Einstürzende Neubauten Einstürzende Neubauten formed in Berlin in 1980 around vocalist and guitarist Blixa Bargeld and percussionist N.U. Unruh. The band’s name translates to “collapsing new buildings,” a reference to construction failures in West Berlin at the time. From the outset, the group built its sound around self-made and adapted instruments, including power tools, scrap metal, oil drums and construction debris, played alongside conventional guitar, bass and vocals. F.M. Einheit joined on percussion before the band’s first LP. The band’s earliest recorded appearance came via the cassette-only “Stahlmusik” in 1980. Einstürzende Neubauten signed to the Hamburg independent label ZickZack, which released “Kollaps” on 5 October 1981, the band’s first official studio album. The record was recorded in Berlin during 1981 and produced by the band itself, with no outside producer credited. Following “Kollaps,” Einstürzende Neubauten continued to record for European independent labels through the 1980s, including “Zeichnungen des Patienten O.T.” (1983) and the compilation “Strategies Against Architecture ’80-’83,” before moving to Some Bizzare/Mute for later releases. Bargeld also worked as a guitarist with Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds from the band’s formation in 1983. Einstürzende Neubauten’s lineup has changed over four decades, with Alexander Hacke and Marc Chung both joining in the years following “Kollaps.” The band added bassist Josefine Lukschy in 2026, alongside confirmed festival dates and studio webcasts. Forty-five years after “Kollaps” introduced the band’s self-made-instrument method on record, Einstürzende Neubauten remains active, with the album standing as the starting point of that catalogue.

items.excerpt: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces.
items.body: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces. We’ll have a full discussion of both nights on this week’s podcast. Okay, admittedly these are shows we’d still be going to even if we didn’t run a website and podcast dedicated to this biz, but we might as well make a meal of it, no? On with this week’s tracks. The Sick Man Of Europe Statiqbloom, “A Grief Observed” Votive, the latest three-track release from now veteran electro-industrial cum dark techno project Statiqbloom does a nice job of triangulating most of the sounds Fade Kainer’s employed under that name over the past decade, from murky half-time power electronics on “Cut The Vine” to more straightforward distorted kicks on “Erased”. But despite its very brief run-time, it’s the sickly acidic programming of “A Grief Observed”, crawling beneath Kainer’s mutters which is reminding us of why we’ve loved his psychedelic approach to vintage post-industrial for so long. Votive by Statiqbloom The Sick Man of Europe, “Apathy” Some pleasingly minimal but still melodic synth action from the UK’s Sick Man of Europe sure is hitting the spot right now. Maybe it’s the insistent drum programming, or the beleeping bass and synthwork, or the punky feedback on the lead, but the contrast between those elements and the frustration and anger of the lyrics certainly gives this one some juice. The Intermittent Signal by The Sick Man Of Europe Nick Viola, “Soft Brutalism” Nick Viola’s name should ring a bell to regular readers, either for his excellent work as Fractured Transmission or his role in the defunct Death Camp Audio clique releases from about a decade back (or his role in US supergroup HexRx, going back further), but a new EP under his own name functions as a good reintroduction to the read on dark techno he’s been working on in recent years. Dense and icy washes of distortion keep the kicks from ever running riot and pushing the subtler cyber programming out of the frame. Soft Brutalism by Nick Viola ᚾᛟᚢ, “Break Like Frost” Nothing Nordvargr finds while digging into his archives is likely to be “pleasant” in any traditional sense of the word. But it’s interesting to hear something like this pulled from the vaults, the first (so far as we can determine) release under the “ᚾᛟᚢ” name, clarifying the nominative distinction between Nordvargr and Trepaneringsritualen’s Thomas Martin Ekelund in their collaborative ᚾᛟᚢ II // ᚦᛟᚦ ᚷᛁᚷ project. Regardless of name or origin the icy mood of this piece’s drifts of death industrial and dark ambient soundscapes are apparent from the moment it begins even without looking at its title, with some classic lo-fi cassette style recording. Trollkorset by ᚾᛟᚢ Then Comes Silence, “Remaker Redeemer” Sweden’s Then Comes Silence make the kind of muscly, synth-inflected goth rock that has never truly gone out of style in Europe. And to their credit, they do it well; where so many acts who attempt the style have neither the vocal charisma nor the hooks to pull it off, TCS has plenty of both to spare. “Remaker Redeemer” has all kinds of mood and atmosphere, but doesn’t skimp on a big jump up chorus, accented by some grindy basswork and syncopated drums that make it fit for the club or the headphones. Requiem Ballroom by THEN COMES SILENCE Ye Gods, “Outlier (single edit)” Oh, to live in a world where songs like Ye Gods’ “Outlier” could be actual radio play singles. Kidding aside, we’re obviously huge fans of Antoni Maiovvi’s work, especially in the sprawling and conceptual esoteric canvas that the producer has made of Ye Gods (hear our interview from last year here), and this cut is no exception. It’s rhythmic, weird, lovely and unnerving, and often both at the same time. New EP Los comes out mid-October, mark it on your halloween calendars. Los by Ye Gods The post Tracks: October 5th, 2027 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Band: Antropoceno | Album: No Ritmo da Terra | Genre: Post-rock | Bandcamp The newest release from this experimental Brazilian act is a harsh and uncompromising record. Taking cues from glitch, avant-garde metal, and native folk, and with lyrics in Portuguese, Tupi, and Yoruba, No Ritmo da Terra is a truly autochthonous Brazilian album. The sound is often maximal, bursting with shining synths, biting guitars and rattling percussion.  Score: 77/100 Band: Beware of Gods | Album: Upon Whom the Last Light Descends III: Behead the Oracle | Genre: Sludge metal, Post-metal | Bandcamp Beware of Gods’ latest album is full of groovy riffs and punishing walls of biting distortion. This band deftly uses texture and atmosphere to paint pictures, and there are a lot of creative and unorthodox choices in how passages and phrases are composed. The sci-fi story the album tells meshes well with the oppressive soundscapes, and this is an instance of things like sound effects and spoken dialogue adding to the effect of the record. Score: 75/100 Band: Haken | Album: in a fever dream | Genre: Progressive metal | Bandcamp This is the most I’ve enjoyed a Haken release since The Mountain. On Haken’s last few LPs, the band had leaned into a form of melodic djent, which, while dazzlingly technical, lacked anything all that memorable, at least to my ear. This new EP sees them take a step back from that and dip their toes back into more Dream Theater-style prog metal. This isn’t just the blatant DT worship of their first two records, though. The band has matured their sound and put their own unique stamp on things. They also include some great moody alt-rock and electronic flourishes, a la Porcupine Tree/Steven Wilson. Score: 85/100 Band: Kolm | Album: Yūgen | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp I like Kolm’s 2018 debut, Umbra, but it is also some of the most blatant and unashamed Tool worship I’ve ever heard. Eight years later, this L.A.-based trio is back with their sophomore album, Yūgen. Yūgen is still obviously deeply indebted to Tool, but the band has diversified their sound a bit. Cynic jumps out as an obvious influence, and they’ve also developed their songwriting and arrangements to be more uniquely their own. My main complaint here is that this is a very long record. A number of riffs and ideas feel drawn out, and the band definitely could have tightened things up. Beyond that, there are a lot of great textures, and the bandmembers are clearly skilled musicians. There are some nice electronic interludes, too. Ignoring the bloat, there’s a lot of good music here. Score: 71/100 Band: Otobo | Album: Inside Machines | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Otobo is a trio from Albany, NY, that plays a crunchy, aggressive band of progressive rock heavily influenced by alt-rock. The songs are all manageable lengths with minimal bloat, but they still contain exciting, dynamic composition. Noise rock, post-punk, and math rock get their turns in the spotlight, too. Otobo does a great job at keeping textures varied, and there’s a skilled balance of complex artiness and enjoyable hooks. The album does lose a bit of steam near the end, but it’s still solid overall. Score: 74/100 Band: Panopticon | Album: Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet | Genre: Post-metal | Bandcamp Billed as a conclusion to a trilogy of records (the others being …And Again into the Light and Rime of Memory), Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet, is another powerful and affecting release in Pantopicon’s discography. The soundscapes swell and bristle, exploding with scouring-yet-abstract black metal riffs. Bluegrass and other forms of American folk music are prominent. Panopticon has a definite sound, so there’s only so much that can be said here that wouldn’t just be describing other records. But this features many of the band’s strongest elements. Score: 82/100

items.body: Toronto-based guitarist, Ayal Senior, developed an approach of listening, playing and collaborating deeply, unhurried and with space (hence the title ‘Yutori‘, which translates to ‘space’) after several creative sojourns to Japan. This philosophy of taking time and patience to create comes through the record’s immeansly laid-back and tranquil dream-folk vibes. The album grew out of of a hushed winter morning session in the recording studio with Senior and several of his friends and collaborators leaning into this almost zen-like method of playing and being in tune with each other. The music’s vast openness and meditative qualities reflect the nature of these sessions, giving them the loose and communal feeling of tight improvised jams. This cooperative energy gives the record a sense of excitement, as it gives the impression the songs can go into any direction at any time. So your ear and attention are hooked right away, and they remain held til the needle reaches the deadwax on Side B. Throughout the album, you are treated to unique variations of instrumental ambient folk that splinters into cosmic string music and astral Americana sounds, with spacey pedal steel, acoustic and fried electric guitar, pearly vibraphones and warm cello. Some tracks are like mini-baroque symphonies, while others lean more into the psychedelic, with dreamlike atmospheric passages and stream of consciousness-styled distorted soloing. The record has the ambiance of a Nick Drake LP, but paired with the looseness and cosmic expansiveness of a Matt Valentine or even a Popol Vuh album. This is especially true with the track that finishes out Side A, “Well of Seven.” Yutori is as serene as a day spent floating around in a still pond, as pastoral as a walk through a freshly snow-covered forest and as illusory and wistful as a half-remembered daydream. If you need a bucolic and peaceful listen to soundtrack your autumn, then this is the album you should reach for. Click here to get your copy on vinyl or digital today. -KH

items.body: Out of all of the underrated bands I know, Boss Keloid have to be among the most underrated. They have many virtues I could sing but the main one is that they just sound like no one else. Their type of winding, dense, and uniquely harmonic stoner/progressive rock is just inimitable. And so, I live between Keloid to Keloid release, craving the very specific flavor that only they can provide. Happily, my latest fix is almost here and good lord is it glorious! Float & Aperture leaves behind a lot of the size and grandiosity of Family The Smiling Thrush and the density of Melted On the Inch in favor of a hard to pin down etherealness. "Pedestal", the second track which I am very pleased to premiere here, will do a better job at explaining what I mean than I can. Check it out below. Float & Aperture by Boss Keloid God, I just love this band. On "Pedestal" you get a taste of the leitmotif which runs through the entire album, some strangely (and pleasingly) sweet, high pitched vocals, and a whole lot of that sound palette that makes Boss Keloid who they are. Which is what exactly? It's that insidious lead guitar line, the fact that I could mean any of the three (at my count) lead guitar lines, the bubbling bass, the way the whole thing feels off-kilter, hazy, and psychedelic to such a unique degree. And finally, it's the excellent lyrics, here (like on the rest of the album) turned very introverted, musing on meaning, intent, self-knowledge, and failure.The entire release is this good. Like "Pedestal", it's angry at times. At others it's alluring, fantastical, strange, self-flagellating, self-aggrandizing, and a few dozens other emotions and perspectives besides. It's similar to previous Keloid releases but also different, uniquely its own thing just like all of their other albums. God I love this band. Please listen to this band! The full thing drops on October 23rd and you can, and should, pre-order it from the Bandcamp page above.

items.body: アメリカ中西部、ウィスコンシン州最大の都市、ミルウォーキー。シカゴから列車で約1時間半、ミシガン湖に面したこのまちに、10年ほど続く「スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキー（Sculpture Milwaukee）」というプロジェクトがあります。その魅力は、年間を通して、第一線で活動する作家の作品に出会えること。非営利団体が主催しながらも、地域の協力や寄付を経て成り立つスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの運営と関係づくりとは？ 本プロジェクトにキュレーターとして参加する竹崎瑞季さんが、3回にわたりレポートします。（artscape編集部） 国を超えて地域をつなぐ 筆者は現在、アメリカ合衆国ウィスコンシン州にある都市、ミルウォーキーに滞在している。令和7年度文化庁新進芸術家海外研修員として2026年2月に渡米し、12月までの約1年弱、ミルウォーキーに滞在する予定である。同地ではパブリック・アートのプロジェクトを展開している非営利団体スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーを研修先として、その戦略や運営についてリサーチするとともに、今年度の展覧会「Power of the Margins」における日本人アーティストのキュレーションに携わっている。 これまで筆者は、香川県にある丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館のキュレーターとして、この場所で見せるべきアーティストや企画とは何かを考え、美術館や地域の特性を生かした展覧会をつくることに努めてきた。出身地である関東から四国に拠点を移して10年が過ぎたが、首都圏に比べて展覧会やアーティストの活動に触れる機会は限られる。一方で、キュレーションを通して離れた地域とつながり、コラボレーションや交流を通して、新たな動きをつくりだしていくことができる可能性を感じていた。 そうしたなかで、スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーについて、ミルウォーキーを拠点とするアーティストであり同プロジェクトのエクゼクティブ・ディレクターを務めるジョン・リーペンホフを通して詳しく知る機会を得た。ミルウォーキーはアメリカ中西部に位置する中規模都市であり、近隣の大都市であるシカゴからは列車で1時間半程度の距離にある。人口面で日本の都市と比較すると、市単位（約56万人）では高松市（約40万人）をやや上回り、都市圏（約157万人）では岡山（約165万人）に迫る規模である。もともと市や州による文化政策が手厚いわけでも、また成熟したアートマーケットが存在するわけでもないアメリカ中西部の地方都市でありながら、第一線で活躍するアーティストを現代的なキュレーションのもとで紹介し、独自のアートシーンを構築している。文化庁の海外研修の支援と、所属美術館の理解を得て実現したこの長期滞在の目的の一つは、プロジェクトの現場に実践的に参与しながらリサーチを行ない、国を超えて異なる地域とつながり、国際的なネットワーク構築の可能性を探ることにあった。 メアリー・ミス《WaterMarks: An Atlas of Water for Milwaukee》（2024） Courtesy of WaterMarks and City as Living Laboratory Project with support from the National Science Foundation. Photography by Michael Lagerman. Originally presented by Sculpture Milwaukee’s exhibition, “Actual Fractals, Act II” (2024-2025). スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーとは まずはその概要について触れておくと、スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーは2017年の設立以来、ミルウォーキーの中心市街地で1年ごとにパブリック・アートの展覧会を開催している団体である。もともとミルウォーキーを拠点に映画館やホテルを運営する企業、マーカス・コーポレーション（The Marcus Corporation）の当時会長であったスティーブ・マーカスの構想を起点に、人々に街の中でアートに触れる機会を提供することを目的に、ミルウォーキー中心市街地改善団体、ミルウォーキー市、地域企業の協力のもとプロジェクトが立ち上げられ、2019年に501(c)(3)★1の資格を認定された非営利団体となった。プロジェクトの主な舞台は、ミシガン湖に面するミルウォーキー美術館の正面エントランスから西に向かって延びる大通り、ウィスコンシン・アベニューを主軸とし、展覧会によって近隣エリアも含めた市内一帯をその活動範囲としている。いずれも24時間365日、街を訪れる人々がいつでも自由にアクセスでき、無料で観覧できる場所に展示され、ミルウォーキーの中心市街地の活性化と文化的土壌の育成に貢献している。 これまで1年に一度のペースで、今年も含めると10回の展覧会が開催され、国内外のアーティストによる作品が展示されてきた。過去の展覧会では、トニー・クラッグやアニッシュ・カプーアなど現代彫刻を代表するアーティストから、ソル・ルウィットやフェリックス・ゴンザレス＝トレスら国際的に注目を集めるアーティスト、トーマス・J・プライスやラシッド・ジョンソンらアフリカ系アメリカ人アーティスト、メグ・ウェブスターやメアリー・ミスら自然環境を扱うアーティスト、トゥルーマン・ローやスカイ・ホピンカら先住民のルーツを持つアーティストなど、幅広い世代と多様なアプローチによる作品が紹介されてきた（これまでの展覧会やキュレーションについては次回詳しく触れたい）。 ソル・ルウィット《Tower (Gubbio)》（1996） Courtesy Pace Gallery, New York. Photography by Kevin J. Miyazaki. Presented by Sculpture Milwaukee’s exhibition (2017). フェリックス・ゴンザレス＝トレス《Untitled (The New Plan)》（1991） Courtesy of the Estate of Felix Gonzalez-Torres. Photography by Michael Lagerman. Presented by Sculpture Milwaukee’s exhibition, “Actual Fractals, Act III” (2025-2026). シカゴ、ミネアポリスのパブリック・アート パブリック・アートという点でアメリカ中西部の他都市の事例と比較してみたい。ミルウォーキーの南に位置し、アメリカ第3の人口規模を誇るシカゴにも多くの作品が存在する。例えば、「The Bean」の通称で世界的にも知られるアニッシュ・カプーアの《Cloud Gate》★2は、中心市街地にあるグラント・パークの一部を再開発するプロジェクトとしてのミレニアム・パークの開園に合わせて2004年に公開された（正式な完成は2006年）。シカゴ美術館（Art Institute of Chicago）に隣接する同園には、ほかにもジャウメ・プレンサらの作品やフランク・ゲーリーの建築が設置され、シカゴの文化的な中心地を形成している。同エリアの南には、マグダレーナ・アバカノヴィッチの106体の彫像による大規模なインスタレーション《Agora》も2006年に設置されている。さらに前史を遡ると、1967年に「Chicago Picasso」の名で親しまれるパブロ・ピカソの《Untitled》★3、1970〜80年代にはアレクサンダー・カルダーやジョアン・ミロなどの彫刻作品が設置された。シカゴはこのようにアメリカでも早い時期から、都市開発の一環としてパブリック・アートが設置され、街の景観が形成されてきたと言える。 ウィスコンシン州の西隣に位置するミネソタ州の最大都市であり、人口規模としてはミルウォーキーよりもやや少ないミネアポリス★4にも、多くの屋外作品が展示されたミネアポリス彫刻庭園（Minneapolis Sculpture Garden）★5が存在する。世界有数の現代美術のアートセンターであるウォーカー・アート・センター（Walker Art Center）とミネアポリス市の行政機関、ミネアポリス公園・レクリエーション委員会（Minneapolis Park and Recreation Board ）★6との連携により1980年代から計画が着手され、1988年に開園、2017年に再整備された。同園のシンボルである巨大なシルバースプーンとチェリーを模った《Spoonbridge and Cherry》（クレス・オルデンバーグとコーシェ・ファン・ブリュッヘンによる共同制作）のほか、マーク・マンダースら約60点を超える作品が、ウォーカー・アート・センターに隣接する約11エーカー（約4.5ヘクタール）の敷地に展示されている。 対してスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの場合、上述のとおりウィスコンシン・アベニューを中心としながらも、ある特定のエリアへの恒久展示が目的ではなく、作品ごとにふさわしい候補地を検討し、アーティストと事務局で協議を重ね、敷地の管理者やオーナーからの協力を経てはじめて展示が決定する。例えば、市が管轄する公園や大通り沿いの歩道から、ミルウォーキー美術館など近隣の文化施設の敷地、ホテルやオフィスビルのエントランス、商業施設の一角や空き店舗のファサードなど、街の文化産業活動を担う多様なプレイヤーとの協働により、広域エリアも含めたさまざまな場所での展示が実現されてきた。 デボラ・カス《OY/YO》（2020） Courtesy of the artist and Kavi Gupta, Chicago. Photography by Sculpture Milwaukee’s exhibition, “there is this We” (2021-2022). エリン・シレフ《Dusk Form》（2024） Courtesy of the artist, Sikkema Malloy Jenkins, and Bradley Ertaskiran. Photography by Michael Lagerman. Presented by Sculpture Milwaukee’s exhibition, “Actual Fractals, Act III” (2025-2026). ハイブリッドなファンドレイジング スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの運営面、特にファンドレイジングに関しては、企業や団体、個人からの寄付がその主軸となっている。文化芸術のための助成ももちろん一つの方法であり、例えば今年度はウィスコンシン州観光局による観光支援プログラム、JEM グラント（Joint Effort Marketing Grant）★7や、アメリカにおける先駆的な女性団体の一つであるウーマンズ・クラブ・オブ・ウィスコンシン（Woman’s Club of Wisconsin）から地域住民向けのアーティスト・トークのための資金提供を受けているが、これらは主に関連イベントや普及活動に充てられるものであり、全体の事業予算のうちで占める割合は小さい。ミルウォーキーでは、市による文化芸術への直接的な予算・助成は、シカゴやミネアポリスと比較して小規模である。先述した近隣都市のパブリック・アートの事例と比較すると、シカゴは公共空間や公共のインフラにアートを取り入れるための行政主導の試みとして、市によるパブリック・アート事業や地域への委託事業を通して発展したものであり★8、ミネアポリス彫刻庭園はミネアポリス市の行政機関とウォーカー・アート・センターの連携である。対して、スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーは中心市街地の企業らによるエリアマネジメントのための団体が主導となり、その後、アートを通して公益に貢献する性質を深め、非営利団体となり活動を続けている。 アメリカでは企業や団体、個人からのドネーションなど、民間による芸術文化への支援が根付いている。もちろん、その時々の政治や経済の状況、また支援者の個別の事情によっても左右され、文化芸術事業を金銭面から支えるファンドレイジングは決して盤石なものではない。スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーでは近年、上述の企業や団体、個人からの寄付のほか、少額からの寄付も含むメンバーシップ制度や、作品販売やコンサルティング、ほかの非営利団体や公共期間からの業務委託などの方法にも取り組んでいる。公共の資金源に頼らず、新たな方法を取り入れながらハイブリッドなファンドレイジングを採用する柔軟性は、スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの運営面での特色の一つと言えるだろう。日本でも寄付による税制控除がないわけではないが、対象となる団体がアメリカよりも限定されており、また芸術への寄付が慣習としても一般的ではないため、民間支援によるファンドレイジングを探るには多くの時間と労力が必要だろう。そうだとしても、アートの枠内での言葉と思考に偏らず、街を動かしているプレイヤーとの関係の構築や、異なる目的意識をもつオーディエンスに向けた言葉やコミュニケーションの回路を開拓していく姿勢には、学ぶべきものが多いことを感じた。 2026年に実施された観光プロジェクト「Milwaukee Art Escape」のポスター https://www.milwaukeeartescape.com/ 生きたプラットフォームとして パブリック・アートのプロジェクトとしてのスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの特徴をいくつか挙げたい。一つ目は、地域を拠点に、国際的に第一線で活躍するアーティストによるクオリティの高い作品を紹介していることである。ニューヨークでもロサンゼルスでもなく、アメリカ中西部の都市であるミルウォーキーで、必ずしも現代アートに親しみのある人々ばかりでないオーディエンスに向けて、優れたアートを通して街の日常の風景をアップデートし続けている。二つ目の特徴は、その年の展覧会で新たに展示される作品と、過去の展覧会で展示された作品が共存している点である。過去に展示された作品の一部は「Legacy Artwork」と呼ばれ、恒久展示作品として街に残り続けている。三つ目は、展覧会を主軸とするプロジェクトの性質に導かれるものでもあるが、その年ごとに、新たなアプローチで地域との連携や普及活動に取り組んでいる点である。例えばミルウォーキー美術館とは、敷地内での展示による連携だけでなく、コロナ禍により一時見合わせていた「ドーセント」と呼ばれるボランティアによる展示解説ガイドと連携したツアープログラムの開発を今年より再開した。また、今年の取り組みとしては、中心市街地の人々やミルウォーキー大学の大学生に向けた交流イベント★9や、州郊外で開催された現代美術のアートフェア、ドア・カウンティ・コンテンポラリー（Door County Contemporary） ★10へのブース出展、アーティストのジョエル・オッターソンとミルウォーキー交響楽団の音楽監督、ケン＝デイヴィッド・マズアによる対談★11、非営利団体のミルウォーキー・フィルム（Milwaukee Film）との連携によるマーティン・シムズの映画上映★12が実施された。今秋にはシカゴ・アートブック・フェア（Chicago Art Book Fair）への出展や、アメリカのモン族支援団体、モン・アメリカン・ウィメンズ・アソシエーション（Hmong American Women’s Association〈HAWA〉）との連携によるパオ・フア・ハーのトークイベント★13も予定されている。公民の別を問わず、新たなコラボレーターとともに、型にとらわれない取り組みでアウトリーチを拡張し続けている。 このようにスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーは、都市開発の流れの中でダイナミックな恒久展示の作品を設置するパブリック・アートのプロジェクトではなく、街と人々とアーティストが織りなす関係性のなかで、プロジェクト自体が柔らかく変化してきたユニークな取り組みであると言える。次回は、生きたプラットフォームとして動き続けるスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーについて、2017年からのキュレーションの変遷とともにこれまでの展覧会を詳しく見ていきたい。 マーティン・シムズ《Find A Way》（2022） Courtesy of the artist and Hoffman Donahue. Photography by Sculpture Milwaukee’s exhibition, “Actual Fractals, Act III” (2025-2026). キム・ミラー《Social Choreography》（2024） Courtesy of the artist. Photography by Menyeneabasi Akpan and Peter Barrickman. Presented by Sculpture Milwaukee’s exhibition, “Actual Fractals, Act Ⅱ” (2024-2025). ★1──スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーは2019年にアメリカの税法上の非課税資格である501(c)(3)を取得した。 ★2──アメリカにおけるアニッシュ・カプーアの最初の屋外作品であるとされる。幅約20メートル、高さ約10メートル、ステンレス製彫刻でその表面に周囲の建築や空、人々を映し出し、シカゴの街のシンボルとして親しまれている。 https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dca/supp_info/chicago_s_publicartcloudgateinmillenniumpark.html ★3──シカゴ市中心部の行政・司法複合施設、リチャード・J・デイリー・センター（Richard J. Daley Center）前の広場に設置されている。高さ約15メートル、施設の外装と同じコールテン鋼で制作された。 https://thedaleycenter.com/the-picasso-2/ ★4──ただし、ミネアポリス市と隣接するセントポール市を合わせた「Twin Cities」の人口（約73万人）はミルウォーキー市の人口を上回る。 ★5──《Spoonbridge and Cherry》などは1988年の開園時に、マーク・マンダースの《September Room》などは2017年の再整備の際に設置された。 https://www.walkerart.org/minneapolis-sculpture-garden/#about-the-garden ★6──ミネアポリス市内の公園管理を行う独立した行政機関。 ★7──JEMグラントの助成を得て、近隣からの観光誘致のプロジェクト「Milwaukee Art Escape」を実施している（2026年8月21日〜10月6日）。 https://www.milwaukeeartescape.com/ ★8──パブロ・ピカソの《Untitled》やアレクサンダー・カルダーの《Flamingo》はシカゴ市や公共機関によって委嘱された作品である。ただし、アニッシュ・カプーアの《Cloud Gate》はシカゴ市によるミレニアム・パークの開発に合わせて設置されたが、その実現には民間企業AT&Tなどからの資金提供を得ている。 ★9──ダウンタウンで働く人々を対象とした「Downtown Employee Appreciation Week」や、UWM（ウィスコンシン大学ミルウォーキー校）の学生を対象とした「The Peck Art School Welcome Back Event」などの交流イベント。 ★10──ウィスコンシン州北東部のドア群で開催された民間のアートフェア。非営利の美術教育施設、ペニンシュラ・スクール・オブ・アート（Peninsula School of Art）を会場とし、2026年6月4日〜7日に開催された。 https://www.doorcountycontemporary.com/ ★11──ジョエル・オッターソンはスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの2025年度の展覧会「Actual Fractals, Act III」の参加アーティストであり、作品はミルウォーキー交響楽団（Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra）の本拠地に展示されている。トークイベントはスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの関連プログラムとして一般に向けて無料で開催された。 ★12──スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの展覧会「Actual Fractals, Act III」（2025-2026）の参加アーティストであるマーティン・シムズの監督映画『The African Desperate』（2022）が、スカルプチャー・ミルウォーキー、ミルウォーキー・フィルム、ブロンズウィル・センター・フォー・ジ・アーツ（Bronzeville Center for the Arts）の連携により上映された。 https://mkefilm.org/films/6a6ce1d8b3889a8985120f60/ ★13──モン・アメリカン・ウィメンズ・アソシエーションは、東南アジア系の女性、BIPOC（黒人、先住民、有色人種）の女性や少女、クィアやトランスジェンダーの人々、モン族系アメリカ人コミュニティを支援する団体。パオ・フア・ハーはスカルプチャー・ミルウォーキーの展覧会「Actual Fractals, Act I」（2023-2024）に参加した、モン族出身のアメリカ人アーティストである。

items.body: 会期：2026/08/01〜2026/09/27 会場：水野美術館［長野県］ 公式サイト：https://mizuno-museum.jp/exhibition/2026-08-exhibiton/ 江戸時代末期から明治時代半ばまで活躍した「最後の浮世絵師」★1月岡芳年（よしとし）（1839-92。最後の画号は大蘇（たいそ）芳年／以下、芳年）の画業を190点の作品を通じて辿る企画展が開催された。企画は日本画を専門とする水野美術館である。筆者が芳年の作品を鑑賞するのは、2012年に東京都の太田記念美術館で開催された「没後120年記念 月岡芳年展」以来である。 なお本展は撮影禁止だったため、ホームページで公開されている作品目録とジャパンサーチをはじめとするデジタルアーカイブ、他館での展示図録などを参照しながら本稿を執筆している。 芳年は歌川国芳の門下生のひとりであり、幕末〜明治維新の過渡期においては無惨絵（血みどろ絵）と呼ばれるセンセーショナルな浮世絵のスタイルを確立し、さまざまな画題を多く手がけてきた。明治時代に入ってからは『報知新聞』で、スキャンダルやゴシップを扱うマスメディア報道の一環として、限られた画面の内に時の事件を劇的にレイアウトした。流血表現のリアリティを増すためにさまざまな色や刷りの工夫がなされていること、西洋画からの影響も取り込んだ写実とデフォルメの中間に位置するような描き方などが特徴的だ。 特に無惨絵についての注目が昭和時代に入ってからも続き、泉鏡花、三島由紀夫、江戸川乱歩とさまざまな作家による言及や、1970年代の回顧展の開催が芳年への注目を押し広げて今日に至る。2012年以降も全国各地の美術館で芳年の展覧会はこれまで多数開催されており、展示作品を西本大氣コレクションから借り受けていることは本展とも共通している。芳年のキャリアを国芳門下の頃から晩年までクロノジカルに見せる展示構成も定石通りだが、ささやかながら大きな差異を生む要素が本展には散見された。 例えば、ホームページや展示会場入口にある「※展示作品の一部に、ショッキングな表現が含まれます」という注意文に加えて、その時期の作品の展示エリアに近づくと動線が二股に分かれたサインが掲示されていた。無惨絵の壁面を経由せず、同時期の異なる画題を鑑賞できるように展示動線が案内されているのである。 展示における配慮や、表現にまつわる自主規制のあり方が年々変化していることも影響しているだろう。しかし、この配慮の存在──キュレーションと言っていいだろう──こそが、芳年の実践において無惨絵を過剰に重視しない展覧会という印象に寄与していたことを記しておきたい★2。広い展示室だから可能な動線設計であり、無惨絵が作品点数が多いなかの一部であることもこの印象を後押ししている。 加えて、これまで展示の機会が少なかったと思われる「東海道名所図絵」（1968）全7点のうち2点が展示されていたことも、本展の重要なキュレーションだろう。「東海道名所図絵」は展覧会のキャプションでも触れられていたように、無惨絵を代表する連作「英名二十八衆句」（1866-67）や「魁題百撰相」（1868）と同時期のものであるとともに、芳年が神経衰弱を発症し休養に入る以前の連作である。本展では、幕末から明治維新にかけての動乱が芳年の神経をすり減らした一因かもしれない、という見立てが示されており、明治天皇の東京行幸（京都から東京への遷都に伴う移動。東幸とも略称される）を描いた本作は、芳年自身が翻弄された時代の変化を描いた作品という点を重視して展示されている。 心の内を推察する材料となる手記や手紙が残っていない作家であるため、神経衰弱を発症した因果については見立ての域を出るものではないかもしれない★3。しかし、無惨絵の連作と「東海道名所図絵」が同時期に描かれていたことは事実である。その事実と、画面に描かれたものについて考えてみる。 （中編へ）※2026年10月6日公開予定 ★1──芳年を紹介するコピーとして多用されているが、初出は雑誌『みづゑ』1973年11月号での「最後の浮世絵師たち」（執筆：小林忠）のようで、芳年を含む同時期の浮世絵師たちを総称したようである。芳年ひとりにコピーとして付いた早い例としては、1976年に大丸京都店で開催された回顧展タイトル「月岡芳年展 最後の浮世絵師」と、雑誌『芸術生活』の1976年5月号の特集「最後の浮世絵師 月岡芳年」が最初期の使用例と思われる。参考：図録『没後120年記念 月岡芳年展』（太田記念美術館、2012）の「月岡芳年 文献目録」（編：日野原健司）を確認。 ★2──“ショッキングな表現”や懸念事項を事前に伝えるトリガーアラートとして、本展のサインは機能していた。芳年についての大々的な展示が始まった1970〜80年代には、おそらくなかったものだろうし、仮にあったとしても、それは（結果的には）無惨絵への期待を煽る機能になっていただろう。 ★3──連作「一魁随筆」（1872）の不評が影響したという説もある。芳年の神経衰弱についてどのような見立てがなされてきたかは今回調査できていない。なお、ソーシャルワークや福祉における「見立て」という言葉は、当事者に起きている症状や取り巻く状況に対する仮説を指しており、その後のコミュニケーションや支援のなかで都度更新されていくことが前提となっている。 鑑賞日：2026/09/12（土）

items.excerpt: 会期：2026/08/05 会場：京都芸術センター 講堂［京都府］ 公式サイト： https://www.kac.or.jp/events/260805/ （前編より） すでに見たように、本作『ジェローム・ベル』の構造の肝は、メタ・ダンスである自作についてのレクチャー・パフォーマンスであり、さらにそれ自体が何重にもねじれたメタ・ダンス性をもつ点にある。パリ・オペラ座バレエ団のバレリーナやマース・カニングハム舞踊団のダンサー、タイ古典舞踊のダンサーなど、「多様なバックグラウンドをもつダンサーが自身について語るドキュメンタリー作品」を制作してきた振付家が、自分自身にそのメソッドを適用しつつ、「本人ではない他者に自伝を語らせる」というねじれや矛盾。ベル自身は、気候変動対策がきっかけであったと述べるが、ここでは、ダンス（舞台芸術）が反復性・再現可能性を前提とすることそれ自体が俎上に乗せられている。 冒頭、舞台に登場した川口隆夫は、前説を述べ、机に座ってノートパソコンを開けると、「私はジェローム・ベルです」とおもむろに自己紹介を始める。「16歳の娘がいます」「今57歳です」「振付家です」。川口自
items.body: 会期：2026/08/05 会場：京都芸術センター 講堂［京都府］ 公式サイト： https://www.kac.or.jp/events/260805/ （前編より） すでに見たように、本作『ジェローム・ベル』の構造の肝は、メタ・ダンスである自作についてのレクチャー・パフォーマンスであり、さらにそれ自体が何重にもねじれたメタ・ダンス性をもつ点にある。パリ・オペラ座バレエ団のバレリーナやマース・カニングハム舞踊団のダンサー、タイ古典舞踊のダンサーなど、「多様なバックグラウンドをもつダンサーが自身について語るドキュメンタリー作品」を制作してきた振付家が、自分自身にそのメソッドを適用しつつ、「本人ではない他者に自伝を語らせる」というねじれや矛盾。ベル自身は、気候変動対策がきっかけであったと述べるが、ここでは、ダンス（舞台芸術）が反復性・再現可能性を前提とすることそれ自体が俎上に乗せられている。 冒頭、舞台に登場した川口隆夫は、前説を述べ、机に座ってノートパソコンを開けると、「私はジェローム・ベルです」とおもむろに自己紹介を始める。「16歳の娘がいます」「今57歳です」「振付家です」。川口自身も振付家としてダンス作品を創作しており（そのなかには、記録映像に基づいて大野一雄の舞踏を完コピする『大野一雄について』［2013］というメタ・ダンス的作品も含まれる）、年齢も近いが、川口は俳優のようにベルを演じているわけではなく、書かれたテキストを日本語で読み上げ、指定された箇所でパソコンを操作して映像を再生させている。舞台上で語られるのは、ダンスをめぐる自作の思索に加え、ダンスとの出会い、エイズによる親友の死、父親になった喜びなどの自伝的語りだが、ベル自身は舞台上には一切姿を現わさず、指定した台詞を他者にしゃべらせ、パソコンを操作させている。ここで顕現するのは、「他者の身体を遠隔操作する」というまさに振付の力学だ。観客は、振付家としてのベル自身についての語りを聞きながら、同時に「他者の身体に及ぼされている振付の作用」そのものを目撃する。 ［Documentation Team © 2026 Hot Summer in Kyoto］ ベル自身、常に「振付（家）という権力性」についてラディカルかつ自己言及的に問うてきたが、本作のタイトル『ジェローム・ベル』は、作品名であると同時に振付家としての署名・・でもある。言い換えれば、この作品は『川口隆夫』ではない。出演者が「その人自身であること」は限りなく希薄化し、消去される。本作は、振付家としての成功も失敗も赤裸々に語られ、失恋や子どもの成長を見守る喜びなど私的な側面も率直に語る、一見誠実なドキュメンタリーでありつつ、完全に非ドキュメンタリーでもある。ここには、「ドキュメンタリー・シアターははたしてどこまで成立可能なのか？」という矛盾した問いも内包されている。一方、本作では、ベル／川口の境界線がわずかに揺らぐ瞬間もある。90年代初めにエイズで友人を亡くしたことが語られるシーンでは、「ダムタイプ」に参加した経歴をもつ川口が、自身の過去を重ね合わせているような沈黙の間があった。 本作はまた、舞台作品の基盤にある反復性や代演可能性を問うとともに、映像アーカイブと舞台芸術の一回性をめぐる問題も内包する。作中では、ダンス作品がスペクタクルな消費社会の速度に抗う抵抗として、繰り返し「今、ここ」にいることの重要性が説かれる。一方、作中で抜粋映像が紹介される自作について、「全編はYoutubeで見れます」と何度も述べられる。「自作についての解説が、それ自体を裏切り、新たな問いを派生させる」という構造がここにもある。 レクチャー・パフォーマンスであり、多層的なメタ・ダンス作品であり、「ドキュメンタリー」の成立（不）可能性をめぐる問いであり、映像アーカイブと舞台のライブ性に対する問いでもある本作。最後に、「クレジット」にも施された仕掛けについて触れたい。「出演」は、川口隆夫だけではなく、「記録映像」で紹介された過去の自作に出演した人物の名前がすべて列挙され、長大なリストをなしている。ここには、「作品の出演者」とは誰を指すのか？ という問いかけとともに、「過去作品に出演した 彼ら全員・・・・とともにこの作品がある」という敬意と誠意が込められている。 鑑賞日：2026/08/05（水） 関連レビュー 未だ見ぬ身体へ──川口隆夫『大野一雄について』｜岡村恵子：フォーカス（2017年11月15日号） 川口隆夫ソロダンスパフォーマンス『大野一雄について』｜高嶋慈：artscapeレビュー（2015年12月15日号）

items.body: The reason I like John Coltrane’s Concert in Japan best out of all my Coltrane albums is that it includes one of my all-time favorite tracks: “Peace on Earth”. And as good as “Meditation/Leo (Part One),” “Leo (Part Two),” and “Part Three” are - “Peace on Earth” outshines them all. When John Coltrane arrived in Japan in 1966, he was welcomed like a king. He arrived at Haneda Airport on July 8, 1966, along with his wife Alice, Pharoah Sanders, Jimmy Garrison, and Rashied Ali. Ali, who later recalled the trip, said they were greeted by thousands of Japanese fans. At the airport, there were huge, life-size cardboard cutouts of the musicians, a red carpet leading from the plane to the terminal, and bouquets of flowers. And Coltrane had a message, it was no coincidence that he wanted to perform in Japan. He insisted on traveling to Nagasaki to visit the Peace Memorial at the site of the atomic bombing. He laid down a wreath and prayed for a long time. The place had a profound emotional and spiritual impact on him. On the evening of his concert in Nagasaki, he played “Peace on Earth” - at that time a new piece and a kind of musical prayer for peace. At a press conference during the tour, when asked about the Vietnam War, he said: “I dislike war, period. It should stop, and any other war.” On Concert in Japan - and on “Peace on Earth” in particular - one can see how Coltrane’s thirst for new sounds is inextricably linked to his desire to view the universe from a spiritual perspective; his music radiates a cosmic aura. The piece begins with an incredibly beautiful melody that floats above Alice’s arpeggios, Garrison’s bass sprinklings, and Ali’s sparse drumming. It seems like the musical embodiment of the Garden of Eden. Nearly six minutes of pure harmony - but then deliberate atonality creeps in, paradise is threatened, only heavenly saxophone lines save it for the time being. Then, however, a dissonant storm is conjured up, shaking this world to its very foundations. The piece is thrown into utter disarray; block chords replace the arpeggios, and the bass and drums throw the meter overboard. At the very end, however, harmony returns, and the melodies resurface, albeit different from how they began. In July 1966, John Coltrane was just one year away from his untimely death, yet his zest for life was greater than ever. His musical explorations were more adventurous than before, and “Peace on Earth” brilliantly captures the essence of what his music is all about. Or, as my friend Thomas Weber puts it: “On the one hand, it’s utter extravagance and exhaustion, on the other, it’s the dissolution of boundaries. Free jazz with melodies.” Email This BlogThis! items.excerpt: 俳優としても活動中の山下幸輝がリーダーを務める5人組ボーイズ・グループの1枚目。全曲にUTAが携わり、〈ありのままでいい〉とポップで華やかな魅力を届ける“EGO”から、切ない失恋を歌った“カスミソウ”、ヒップホップやロックの要素を散りばめた“Make rules”という異なる色のユニット曲まで、ヴァラエティに富んだナンバーに挑み、ポテンシャルの高さを感じる充実作。

items.excerpt: 2年ぶりのアルバムは、昨年のガーナ〜南ア探訪を契機としてアフリカン・ルーツを捉え直し、黒人女性としての誇りや美意識を表明。元D12のミスター・ポーターを総轄役に、マッドリブのビートにも乗りながら自己愛やコミュニティをテーマに力強く澱みないフロウを披露する姿にはコンシャスMCとしての矜持が光る。ディアンジェロ“One Mo’ Gin”使いのネオ・ソウル“Apple Juice”では官能を歌い、後半部でジョージ・クリントンが語る“OMG! items.body:
Creepy Nuts brought Japanese hip-hop to the National Stadium, opening the Singapore leg of The Weeknd’s After Hours Til Dawn Tour with a set of anime favourites, club beats and turntable flourishes.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Creepy Nuts (@creepynuts_official)

Rapper R-Shitei and DJ Matsunaga make a compelling double act. R-Shitei packs his verses with quick, tightly controlled syllables, while Matsunaga cuts into the beats with scratches and rhythmic accents. Their sound gives the ear plenty to follow: the pace of the rapping, the shifting percussion and the hooks that emerge from all that activity.

‘Biriken’ opened the set with a bouncing Jersey club rhythm, followed by ‘Yofukashi no Uta’ and the jazzy ‘Daten’. The mood grew darker with ‘doppelgänger’ and ‘Chxxai’, whose pounding beats and electronic textures brought the selection closer to a late-night club set.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Creepy Nuts (@creepynuts_official)

A dedicated DJ routine gave Matsunaga the spotlight midway through. Scratching, quick cuts and beat juggling are central to his performance style, making the decks an instrument with their own rhythmic voice. The placement gave both halves of the partnership their due before the instantly recognisable ‘Bling-Bang-Bang-Born’.

From there, the duo moved through ‘Mirage’, ‘Fright’ and ‘Nidone’, saving ‘Otonoke’ for last. The DAN DA DAN opening theme was a crowd favourite, rounding off their energetic set before The Weeknd took the stage.

items.body:
pami explores why knowing better doesn’t always mean walking away on her latest single, ‘loser’.

Released on 30 September, the Thai singer-songwriter’s track follows someone caught in an on-and-off situationship, choosing an unfulfilling connection over the prospect of being alone. Feelings linger even when commitment remains elusive, leaving its protagonist willing to accept another disappointment just to keep someone close.

Co-written by pami and Jett Blyton, with production by Maribelle, ‘loser’ took shape at a songwriting camp in Australia. Its demo was written and produced in a single day, following a conversation between the songwriters about their own experiences of unhealthy and disappointing relationships.

That shared experience informs the song’s central dilemma: recognising a hurtful pattern can be easier than finding the resolve to leave it. Through its story of teenage romance, ‘loser’ examines the gap between wanting genuine affection and settling for what is available.

Hailing from Phuket, pami works across bedroom pop and indie, pairing personal storytelling with atmospheric melodies. She debuted under Juicey in 2024 and released her first full-length album, puffette, the following year. Her catalogue includes ‘pity dirty’, ‘kiss me blue’, and this year’s ‘cry jar’ and ‘all in’.
