items.body:
Charlie Lim is heading back to Manila after seven years, with a new collaboration arriving ahead of his visit.

The Singaporean singer-songwriter will hold an intimate showcase of his latest album, DAYDREAM, at ANALOG MNL, Rockwell Center, Makati, on 11 October. Featuring a vinyl listening session and an exclusive performance, the event will also see him joined by Clara Benin and Young Cocoa.

Fans can sign up for an invitation here.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Charlie Lim 林宇 (@wherewascharlie)

Lim last performed in Manila at Wanderland Music Festival in 2019. This time, he is looking forward to sharing his music in a smaller setting.

“Festivals are always exciting, but there’s something different about being in a smaller room where you can actually sit with the songs and have a proper conversation with people,” he shares. “DAYDREAM is a very personal record, so being able to share it that way feels quite fitting.”

Ahead of the showcase, Lim will release a new version of ‘One Day I’ll Learn’ featuring Young Cocoa at midnight on 7 October. The Filipino rapper contributes an additional verse to the DAYDREAM track, offering his own perspective on regret, self-reflection, and learning from past mistakes.

“What made the collaboration really interesting to me was that Young Cocoa brought a perspective I would not have naturally arrived at on my own,” Lim explains. “His verse really gives the song another voice and another way of looking at that idea.”

Young Cocoa approached the track by listening without reading its lyrics first, allowing his emotional response and personal experiences to guide his writing. Lim’s openness also gave him room to experiment.

“I remember telling him I might get weird with it or experimental, and there was no opposition from his end,” the rapper says. “I relish and thrive when I get to explore all the creative pathways, and having Charlie be encouraging and generally laid-back throughout the process made it easy.”

The pair worked remotely, with Young Cocoa’s melodic choices making a particular impression on Lim.

“I couldn’t stop smiling when he sent over the demo; he really took it to another place, and I am so honoured to have such a talent hop on a song from DAYDREAM.”

Lim will also participate in FILSCAP’s Asia Songwriting Master Camp 2026, joining songwriters from across the region.

On 2 October, the opening night of his Singapore After Hours Til Dawn Tour shows, Abel Tesfaye performed to 55,000 fans across a two-hour, 39-song set. Giant sculptures, lasers, and fire gave his songs a suitably outsized setting, while his frequent shout-outs and trips toward
items.body:
Eight years is a long time between visits. For The Weeknd, it was enough to turn a Singapore Indoor Stadium audience of 7,000 into two sold-out nights at the National Stadium, with a catalogue of new sing-alongs to match.

On 2 October, the opening night of his Singapore After Hours Til Dawn Tour shows, Abel Tesfaye performed to 55,000 fans across a two-hour, 39-song set. Giant sculptures, lasers, and fire gave his songs a suitably outsized setting, while his frequent shout-outs and trips towards the crowd made room for more personal exchanges.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

Before the main event, Japanese hip-hop duo Creepy Nuts warmed up the stadium with a set that included ‘Otonoke’, their theme song for DAN DA DAN. The anime favourite helped get the audience moving ahead of a night that would cover much of Tesfaye’s musical history.

He arrived in black, his face concealed by a glittering mask that projected green laser beams, opening with ‘Baptized In Fear’ from Hurry Up Tomorrow. It was an introduction that established the show’s visual language immediately: an imposing, futuristic world with a recognisable voice at its centre.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

That world stretched across the stadium. A backdrop of ruined buildings framed the main stage, with long runways connecting separate performance areas. At the middle stood a rotating, 12-metre golden robot sculpture by Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama. Dancers in red robes and gold masks moved through the space, keeping the production in motion as Tesfaye travelled between stages.

Out in the audience, synchronised LED wristbands extended the light show into the stands. Lasers swept overhead, strobes punctuated the music, and bursts of flame added heat to the spectacle. The staging gave fans several places to look, even as the songs kept their attention fixed on the singer.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

The set moved through the different sounds that have brought The Weeknd this far: the darker R&B of ‘House Of Balloons’, the pop immediacy of ‘Can’t Feel My Face’, and the synth-driven rush of ‘Blinding Lights’. With nearly 40 songs packed into two hours, the pace left little room for pauses or a conventional encore.

There was plenty of space for his voice, though. ‘The Hills’ and ‘Call Out My Name’ called for forceful delivery, while ‘Take My Breath’ and ‘Sacrifice’ pushed into his upper register. On ‘Out Of Time’, which he introduced as a personal favourite, the focus shifted to the phrasing and vibrato that give his R&B performances their character.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

The crowd met the hits with dancing and full-volume choruses. ‘Starboy’ and ‘Blinding Lights’ brought fans in the seated sections to their feet, while ‘One Of The Girls’, originally recorded with JENNIE and Lily-Rose Depp, became a particularly loud audience showcase. As the accompaniment gave way, thousands of voices carried its chorus across the stadium.

For all the ominous imagery surrounding him, Tesfaye spent much of the evening showing Singapore affection. Around 20 minutes into the set, he removed his mask, smiled, and greeted the audience with an air hug. He repeatedly worked the city’s name into his songs, including ‘Faith’ and ‘Save Your Tears’, turning familiar lyrics into greetings for the crowd in front of him.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

He also headed down towards fans on the floor several times, offering the microphone for sing-alongs. Those exchanges gave the concert a different kind of scale: a show built for tens of thousands could still make someone at the barricade part of the performance.

By the time the set finished, Singapore had heard how much The Weeknd’s catalogue had expanded since his last visit and seen how confidently he could carry it into a stadium. The towering robot and laser-eyed mask supplied the imagery, but the unaccompanied roar of ‘One Of The Girls’ supplied something the production could never programme.

items.body:
GENERATIONS are taking on their own dancefloor legacy with ‘VIBE’.

Released digitally on 28 September, the EDM-driven single was created to stand alongside ‘AGEHA’, a defining track for the Japanese group released a decade ago. A physical release follows on 28 October, marking their first CD single in four years.

Member Alan Shirahama co-wrote and arranged ‘VIBE’, working alongside TET$V and Kanata Okajima. The track draws on the dance sound long associated with GENERATIONS and LDH, combining a propulsive beat and an immediate hook with moments designed for fans to shout along at concerts and festivals.

“It's something only GENERATIONS, and only LDH, can really pull off, and over time I think it's stopped being ‘the sound of that era’ and become something closer to a sound that's genuinely ours, one with lasting value,” Shirahama shared. “But we didn't just want to repeat it, we packed in things that still feel fresh inside that same DNA.”

The accompanying music video places live-action footage of all six members against backgrounds and environments created using generative AI. Dance takes centre stage, with choreography developed specifically for the video and a sliding sequence from vocalist Ryuto Kazuhara among its featured moments.

‘VIBE’ also arrives ahead of the group’s 15th anniversary year, which begins in November. For Shirahama, the song’s opening line sets the tone for what comes next.

“Opening the song with the line ‘this is where the good part starts’ is both a declaration and a challenge to ourselves,” he explained. “It's not an aggressive track either, there's a sense of ease that comes from having grown up, but we also built in moments where the audience can shout along with us live.”

All six members marked the release with a LINE livestream, sharing stories around VIBE-themed topics. The broadcast drew more than one million total views.

MANG x DAOU are taking ‘Aroma’ to the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

The duo won Thailand’s Chosen One, the country’s national selection show, at Centerpoint Entertainment in Bangkok on 27 September. They will represent host nation Thailand at the Grand Final at One Bangkok Forum on 14 November, competing alongside artists from 10 other countries.

MANG, LIT Entertainment’s first female solo artist, brings powerful vocals and a T-pop sound infused with Thai influences. DAOU Pittaya is a singer, actor, and MC who took first place on LazIcon. Their collaboration draws on both artists’ strengths while placing Thai culture at its centre.

“We’ve put so many Thai elements into the song, and we hope people in other countries will discover what Thailand is through it,” said MANG. “This is a moment in history for me and one of the greatest opportunities of my life. We’re so excited, and we’ll do our very best.”

DAOU added: “Our culture has so many different sides that we can share, and now that we’ve won, we’ll do everything we can to represent Thai style on this big stage. Thailand is the host, and we want to make it a surprise for everyone.”

The duo join representatives selected from Bhutan, the Philippines, South Korea, Laos, and Malaysia. The national selection schedule also includes Nepal Decides on 7 October, Mongolia’s Chosen One on 10 October, and Cambodia’s Finest Voice on 17 October. Fans can watch the selection shows on the Eurovision Song Contest YouTube channel and vote through the Eurovision Asia website.

For fans heading to Bangkok, general ticket sales opened on 2 October, following a Eurofan presale the day before. Tickets are offered for both the televised Grand Final and a Preview Show rehearsal, with access through Thailand Megatix:

Grand Final: Prices start at approximately THB 1,670

Preview Show rehearsal: Prices start at approximately THB 1,170

“Eurovision Song Contest Asia provides a unique platform for artists from across the region to showcase their music, creativity and cultural identity on one stage,” said Executive Producer Assaf Blecher. “We are delighted to welcome Thailand’s chosen representatives to One Bangkok Forum this November, where they will compete alongside artists from 10 other countries across the region.”

items.body:
Clavin Cher took home the Best Song Award for ‘All Is Well’ at the SG:SW I Write The Songs 2026 Finale Concert, as the Mandarin songwriting festival celebrated its 10th anniversary.

Held on 3 October at the Singapore Chinese Cultural Centre’s Far East Organisation Auditorium, the finale saw the top 10 finalists perform their original compositions before a judging panel and close to 350 audience members. 10 representatives from past editions opened the evening with a performance of the festival’s theme song.

Clavin Cher

Returning for his third SG:SW, Cher wrote both the melody and lyrics for ‘All Is Well’, which pairs a dark rock arrangement with reflections on a world in turmoil and the hope that love can offer. The judges praised his handling of the social theme and the arrangement’s emotional impact. Cher previously received the festival’s Lyrics (Merit) Award in 2023.

Wong Yijuin and Kenta received the Melody (Merit) Award for ‘Falling For You’, an electronic-infused love song co-composed by the pair, with lyrics by Wong. After four years of participating in SG:SW, Wong reached the top 10 with a song exploring the excitement and uncertainty of falling in love.

Wong Yijuin and Kenta

The year’s youngest duo, lyricist Anne Chua and composer Ho Mei Xuan, picked up both the Lyrics (Merit) Award and Popularity Award (Public Voting) for ‘Spot’. Their new-age composition celebrates fleeting moments and finding joy in the present. The song received 1,470 public votes, marking another Popularity Award win for Ho, who also claimed the honour in 2024.

Ho Mei Xuan and Anne Chua

‘Demolished’, composed by Edmund Ng with lyrics by Lee Jia Min and performed by Janelle Chen, earned the Best Vocal Performance Award. Exploring the difficulty of letting go as a relationship changes, the song continues a creative partnership between Ng and Lee that began after they met at SG:SW in 2020. The pair previously won the Lyrics (Merit) Award for ‘Would You Stay’ in 2022.

Edmund Ng, Lee Jia Min and Janelle Chen

Rounding out the six awards, ‘Inked in Time’ won the Best Performing Band Award. Composed by Gresilda Tan with lyrics by Ang Min Jia, the song was the top 10’s only Oriental Pop entry, featuring live guzheng and flute performances. Its lyrics use painting as a metaphor for longing, waiting, and reunion.

Gresilda Tan and Ang Min Jia

Co-organised by Singapore Chinese Cultural Centre (SCCC), Ocean Butterflies Music, and the Composers & Authors Society of Singapore (COMPASS), this year’s festival received 239 song entries from 223 participants.

A new team-based format saw local singer-songwriters and festival ambassadors Yokez and Ben Hum each mentor 12 finalists over four months, offering guidance on songwriting, arrangement, and stage presentation. Both also performed as guests at the finale.

The top 24 finalists appeared at the festival’s Live Showcase at Bugis+ Atrium in August, which drew 23,240 attendees across two days, its largest turnout to date. The top 10 then attended the festival’s first Songwriting Camp, with workshops and a masterclass led by Mandopop songwriter-producer Real and songwriter Tina Wang. The youngest top 10 finalist was 16.

Real and Wang also joined Dr Liang Wern Fook, Zennon Goh, and Zhong Kunhua on the finale’s judging panel.

“For a decade, SG:SW has nurtured a new generation of local songwriters, giving promising newcomers a stage to grow and be heard,” said Ocean Butterflies Music Managing Director Colin Goh. “Their spirit of ‘daring to write, sing and be different’ brings the fresh energy and voice that Mandopop needs.”

items.body:
For XD:I, the show extends well beyond a three-minute song.

Made up of SWAN, BETTY, HAZÈ, and KANA, the four-member girl group combine K-pop vocals, rap, and choreography with DJing and electronic music. Their live format revolves around a continuous set, with members moving between the decks and the main stage as they build the crowd’s energy.

Represented by THE ARK Foundation, XD:I have been developing that approach through club and party performances in Seoul, including a 40-minute live set at Jangchung Gymnasium in August. Their recent festival bookings included EDC Korea’s circuitGROUNDS stage on 3 October, bringing the project into the electronic music festival circuit.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by XD:I (@way2_xdi)

K-pop listeners may already recognise SWAN as Shin Jiyoon, formerly of Weeekly. A songwriter and composer as well as a performer, she brings her idol experience into a role that now includes DJing and longer festival sets. Her artist profile also details solo work spanning lyric writing, composition, arrangement, choreography, and styling.

Alongside her at the decks is BETTY, whose background includes club appearances and a runner-up placing at the PLIT DJ Competition. She moves between DJing, rap, MCing, and dance, helping maintain momentum and respond to the audience throughout the set.

HAZÈ adds vocals, rap, and performance to the mix. Her profile describes a more restrained approach to expression, offering a different presence within the group. Youngest member KANA contributes vocals and dance, highlighted by her clear vocal tone and expressive delivery.

Those individual strengths feed into a flexible approach to performing. SWAN and BETTY handle DJing, while all four contribute across the show, with their roles changing according to the track and the flow of the set. Songs connect through electronic sections, choreography, and crowd interaction, giving the members room to develop a performance over a longer stretch of time.

“XD:I has been developed as a group that can connect DJing, vocals, rap, choreography, performance and direct audience interaction within one continuous set,” says Chanjae Park, CEO of THE ARK Foundation. “Each member has a different strength, and those different strengths come together to create the full XD:I live experience.”

For an introduction to their recorded music, there’s ‘SPRAY U’. Released on 5 August, the tech house-based single establishes the electronic direction underpinning the group’s live concept.

XD:I plan to take that format to more clubs and international festivals while continuing to release music as a K-pop group. Their ambition is to make the transitions between the decks, the microphone, and the choreography part of what fans come to see.

items.body:
Mark Tuan is letting his playful side shine on ‘NIGHTLIGHT’.

Released on 2 October via Transparent Arts and DNA, the alternative pop track features Thai artist MILLI and serves as the second single from the GOT7 member’s forthcoming album, following ‘Alone’.

Written during a trip to Nashville, ‘NIGHTLIGHT’ pairs Tuan’s vocals and rap with groove-driven production, exploring attraction, curiosity, and the excitement of pursuing what you want. MILLI joins him with a verse that switches between Thai and English.

“I’d been seeing fans ask for more rap, so when I went into the session in Nashville, I really wanted to play around with that side of myself,” Tuan shares. “After ‘Alone,’ which was more introspective and focused on feeling closed off, I wanted ‘NIGHTLIGHT’ to feel like a shift: more open, playful and in motion.”

The collaboration also took the song in an unexpected direction for Tuan, whose solo catalogue has featured relatively few guest artists.

“When she sent her verse back, it was completely different from what I had imagined, but in the best way,” he says of MILLI’s contribution. “It opened up a whole new set of ideas for the song, even visually.”

“Hearing Thai and English alongside each other also made the record feel bigger and more dynamic. It became something neither of us would have made on our own.”

Member Takumi Kawanishi co-composed the title track, ‘ANIMAL’, a high-energy dance number about letting out the side of yourself you usually keep hidden. Fans previously got a preview of the song at KCON LA and ROCK IN JAPAN FESTIVAL ahead of its release.

The accompanying music video takes that idea literally, following JO1 as they escape a “cage” and venture into an unpredictable world. It culminates in a large-scale performance sequence with 30 dancers joining the group.

The EP’s release coincided with the start of JO1’s North American tour stop at Toronto’s Danforth Music Hall. The five-date run also takes in New York, Chicago, and San Francisco before wrapping up on 11 October at The Novo in Los Angeles.

items.excerpt: “There are black silences, like thunderclouds, that burst into flashes of music,” H. G. Wells writes in Select Conversations with an Uncle. items.body: “There are black silences, like thunderclouds, that burst into flashes of music,” H. G. Wells writes in Select Conversations with an Uncle. The phrase finds an almost literal visual counterpart in Jordan Reyes’s cover for Songs for Sad Poets Vol. III: a dense black expanse pressing against a bleached, nearly featureless sky, its uneven boundary resembling storm clouds seen in negative. It also anticipates a pivotal moment in “Sigils of Decay”, when the music comes to such an abrupt halt that, on first hearing, I had to check whether it was still playing. Out of that prolonged absence a low rumble eventually emerges, giving voice to the disquiet that runs through the latest collaboration between Siavash Amini & Eugene Thacker. The three pieces included are dedicated respectively to Vietnamese poet Hàn Mặc Tử, Brazilian Symbolist João da Cruz e Sousa and Austrian poet Nikolaus Lenau, figures connected by the tradition of the poète maudit. “Leprous Doubt”, for Hàn Mặc Tử, opens with dissonant textures, degraded sounds and sudden changes of register. It is unsettling and unsettled, meandering in unforeseen directions and making its discomfort palpable. The music pauses and resumes, pitching antagonistic forces against one another; moments of sweeping grandeur coexist with passages of intimate travail. It repeatedly attempts to steady itself before faltering again. Circular tones eventually lift to reveal the “glowing abyss” of Thacker’s poem, while intensifying drones recede until a solitary, quivering tone remains. “Sigils of Decay”, for Cruz e Sousa, pushes this instability into silence itself. The long interruption at its centre makes the eventual return of sound unusually physical. As the low frequencies slowly reassert themselves, muted fragments accumulate into a dark, suspended mass. Thacker writes of “muted music / woven by / night spiders”, an image that seems uncannily close to what Amini constructs: strands of sound gradually spun into a crepuscular firmament of drones and disarticulated fragments, only to loosen again. The connection with Cruz e Sousa is equally suggestive. His poetry transforms an inexplicable melancholy into a confrontation with the Infinite; Thacker condenses that metaphysical sadness into the colder “Dread of / Infinite space. / Dread of / Distant skies.” At nineteen minutes, “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” is the album’s most expansive piece. Its opening is nocturnal, with celestial voices suspended above slumbering coils of sound. These gradually precipitate into increasingly abrasive textures, yet the music pulls itself back towards a softer harmonic balance. Timbral shifts become more pronounced as the underlying material turns metallic and resonant. Lenau’s recurring world of night, forests, barren landscapes, grief and death finds an oblique counterpart here: the landscape seems to have been emptied of narrative and retained as atmosphere, shadow and distant light. Voice assumes a much greater presence than on the first Songs for Sad Poets, although words never present themselves as intelligible text. Synthetic voices gather into spectral choirs and dissolve into the surrounding music, allowing Thacker’s poems to remain embedded within the pieces without requiring the listener to follow them line by line. The relationship between poetry and sound consequently operates through images, structures and emotional pressure: Hàn Mặc Tử’s diseased bodies and impossible skies, Cruz e Sousa’s metaphysical melancholy, Lenau’s nocturnal desolation. Each piece finally leaves a coda of silence. By then, Reyes’s cover feels increasingly inseparable from the music: darkness occupies most of the field, while its opposite persists beyond its ragged edge. H.G. Wells’s “black silences” provide an apt description of an album where silence continually threatens to swallow the music, yet also provides the space from which it can begin again. To lift the veil on the production process we have spoken directly to Saivash Amini. On the first Songs for Sad Poets, Eugene Thacker’s poems were never actually spoken; the words were translated into sound without becoming voice. On Vol. III, you take almost the opposite route, programming voice-synthesis software to perform the poems and then processing as many as forty voices until language becomes unintelligible. What interested you in bringing the human voice into the project only to erase its legibility again? Do you still think of these pieces as songs, or has the distinction between voice, text and sound become irrelevant? The idea of voice synthesis came out of a conversation with Eugene about his dislike of the human voice and the vocal music he actually liked like Ligeti’s requiem, where micropolyphony, among other techniques, were used to mask the intelligibility of the text and transform the human choir into something entirely different. I have much of the liberty of a large choir in my DAW with voice synthesis software. It’s not actually a human voice, so I can make a sound very modulated and affected when singing. And I can have as many as I want to have, as long as my CPU can handle it, so micropolyphony can be much more extreme and differently intricate. And yes, I do think of these as songs, they are structured around the poem. Just not conventional songs with known musical structures. But that’s when I’m making them. There’s no point trying to find the points of reference to poems if you’re just listening, they are trying to convey the same thing. Listening closely to the three pieces, decay seems to function as a compositional process rather than simply as an atmosphere. “Leprous Doubt” repeatedly loses substance and regains it; “Sigils of Decay” moves through accumulation and withdrawal; and the nineteen-minute “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” forms large masses of sound that gradually weather away, return and finally disappear. This concern with appearance, erosion and reconstitution also seems connected to Eidolon, Caligo and Severed Like the Red Moon, where sounds are made to float, bleed, collapse, be mutilated and reassembled. Has this become a central way for you to think about musical form? Yes and no, I have been more and more putting focus in making structures and out evolving and directional textures made out of different approaches to generating harmony. It’s not all I think about when making pieces but more likely the result of intentional putting together of smaller directional elements of different duration. So the micro is what determines the macro, and a lot of the times I’m thinking of micro. The poets invoked on Vol. III come from very different linguistic and cultural histories: Hàn Mặc Tử and Vietnam’s “Chaos” school, João da Cruz e Sousa and Brazilian Symbolism, and Nikolaus Lenau and the tradition of Weltschmerz. How did you and Eugene Thacker arrive at these particular figures, and what drew you to bringing such different poetic traditions together within the same musical cycle? That’s all Eugene’s side of the project but the thread that links them all is in the Poet Maudit term which the title comes from. They all fit that category. Much of your recent work has begun from literary or historical material: Ibn Sina on eremos, Xavier Villaurrutia on The Sweat of Earth, early Iranian piano recordings and Malakoot on Caligo, as well as Houshang Golshiri on Severed Like the Red Moon. In each case, the source seems to act less as something to illustrate than as a force that changes the way you treat sound. What does literature give you that a purely musical starting point does not, and has worked so closely with Eugene Thacker altered the way you now read a text as a composer? Using literature for my work goes to my first album. Then I have three collaborations with Matt Finney which were based on his reading his poems and sending them to me. Serus had a strong relationship with the writings of Blanchot I can go on… I find using literature gives me a structure and image which I can turn into sound worlds. I can imagine something to convey that image. I find that very exciting but a lot of background work before the project starts is done on purely musical material. Working with Eugene changed my workflow in general and made my relationship with literature deeper than it was before, and it gave me a lot to think about when it comes to making sound that conveys what one word is telling me. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: God Is Everything You Are Not is built from voice, MicroKORG synthesis, a microphonic soundbox from LeafAudio, and field recordings. Seven pieces, just under 36 minutes. The release notes describe grief approached as passage rather than narrative, and that framing holds, this record puts you inside the duration of something rather than telling you it happened. Voice-forward, inward-facing, unconcerned with visibility God Is Everything You Are Not by Elika Ostrov   Fort Evil Fruit is a small Irish imprint that consistently operates in spaces most labels avoid, quiet, uncomfortable, structurally unconventional work sitting between sound art and song. Elika Ostrov fits that context without friction. Outside of this release there’s very little information available on her, which feels appropriate given how the record presents itself: voice-forward, inward-facing, unconcerned with visibility. God Is Everything You Are Not is built from voice, MicroKORG synthesis, a microphonic soundbox from LeafAudio, and field recordings. Seven pieces, just under 36 minutes. The release notes describe grief approached as passage rather than narrative, and that framing holds, this record puts you inside the duration of something rather than telling you it happened. “Candy Apple Pie” opens things and it’s the track that pulled me in first. Her voice carries the whole weight of the piece, sitting on top of what sounds like lightly bitcrushed synth underneath. There’s something almost melodic about it, almost settled. One of the warmer moments on the record, which catches you off guard given what the album is called. From there things get quieter and darker. “Kapu” sustains that shift without forcing it—the synth texture recedes further into the background noise and the grief the album orbits starts to feel more present, less described. It doesn’t announce itself. None of these pieces follow any conventional structure. Rhythms don’t materialize. Nothing locks in. The whole thing sounds loosely assembled, and that’s the point, the album is designed to feel like something you’re moving through rather than observing. Background is the compositional choice, not a byproduct of it. The title track runs 16:45 and arrives at the end like a separate document entirely. Ringing ambience opens it, sustained long enough that it starts to accumulate into something disorienting. Running underneath that is a static interference noise, the exact frequency you’d get from a phone sitting too close to a receiver, that ticking electrical feedback. That specific texture generates most of the tension in the piece. Ostrov speaks throughout but the audio is reversed, her voice present and completely inaccessible at the same time. You hear her talking for the full duration without understanding a word. Then, toward the end, the audio flips forward and you can actually hear her. Sixteen minutes of building toward a moment it never telegraphed. That ticking electrical feedback :: The closest reference points for the record’s overall aesthetic are somewhere between the warped loop logic of Dat Politics, the peculiar stillness of Boards of Canada at their most unsettling, and the indie-adjacent vocal sensibility of Noriko Tujiko. Ostrov shares certain instincts with all three without directly resembling any of them. The reverse-to-forward reveal on the title track stays with you after the record ends. Grief made audible as a structural decision, not a theme. Experimental electronic music has always found its most interesting moments when artists stop treating it as a genre and start treating it as a method. The tools shift, tape gave way to DAWs, DAWs gave way to modular, modular gave way to whatever hybrid setups artists are running now, but the impulse underneath stays the same. Find a way to make the listener feel something the conventional song structure can’t reach. Ostrov is working in that tradition without announcing it. The MicroKORG and the LeafAudio soundbox and the reversed vocals aren’t chosen for their novelty. They’re chosen because they do specific things to time and memory and presence that a guitar and a verse-chorus wouldn’t. That’s what keeps this corner of music alive, artists who use the tools as extensions of the idea rather than the idea itself. God Is Everything You Are Not is exactly that kind of record. God Is Everything You Are Not is available on Fort Evil Fruit. items.body: wave_function ultimately displays an artist working in top form, mapping out a series of experimental electronic terrains that converge into something uniformly disjointed, immersive, and quietly mind-bending. Broken sonic relics, elastic and stretched to their limits wave_function by Marco Simioni   One of our favorite mechanized glitch-electronic artists, Marco Simioni, returns with wave_function for Barcelona-based Evel, an imprint that continues pushing fractured, futuristic sound-scrapes from artists across the planet. Simioni digs miles and miles into erratic, densely packed rhythmic DSP-laden structures, shaping minimalist extrusions that echo, bend, and arch. Opener “et II no pt re” feels as though its pulsing tone and abrasive grit could push straight through the cosmos. Corrupted sonic data, indeed. Simioni works in infinitesimal layers, carefully weaving hypnotic electro-glitch hybrids into shifting forms and textures. Tracks like “yttr flux” and “vinh 49” emerge as broken sonic relics, elastic and stretched to their limits, while “pulse array for dissolving realities (dive mix)” moves through a restrained ambient propulsion, industrial drone filaments threading through the mix like fragments of an unknown message waiting to be deciphered. “ekkot vire” pushes deeper into abstract electronic substructures, constantly expanding, collapsing, and reforming, before “509dualech2211eren” loops through a haze of ambient flutter, surrounding the listener with microscopic details of tone, drone, and white noise. The ending highlights Simioni’s ability to cultivate tiny, ethereal sound forms that remain ruptured at their edges while maintaining the pulse of a living machine. wave_function ultimately displays an artist working in top form, mapping out a series of experimental electronic terrains that converge into something uniformly disjointed, immersive, and quietly mind-bending. elseq fans should take immediate notice. wave_function is available on Evel. items.excerpt: The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other. &nbs
items.body: The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other.   Consumers finds its second wind Manic by Drift   Alive & Thriving by Radius Etc   There’s a good story behind why this review exists at all. The Consumers Research and Development Label ran independently through the 2000s before becoming an imprint of Someoddpilot Records, the Chicago label-turned-agency that also handled branding for Pitchfork back when that meant something specific in the industry, and later built brand identity work for clients like Drag City, Jagjaguwar, and Secretly Canadian. Geoffrey Wilson bought Consumers in 2023 with help from Chris Eichenseer, who founded Someoddpilot in 1999 and who Wilson had shared an office with from 2003 to 2008, before the label originally shut down. Somewhere in the years between closing and reopening, a flood destroyed the entire back stock. Whatever’s floating around on Discogs or eBay now is all that survived physically; the rest is gone. The label came back properly in November 2024 with a showcase at Public Works in Wicker Park, quiet after that, and this is its real reintroduction to a wider audience: two EPs, two very different sounds, one label figuring out what it wants to be the second time around. Drift’s Manic comes first and it’s a strange kind of debut for someone who’s clearly not new to any of this. Sean Krainik has run Parotic Records, the Midwest techno label, for over two decades, putting out records from DJ Slip, Johannes Heil, Matt Paffel, Dave Olson, and Mr. Projectile among others. He never released his own music on vinyl until now. Manic pulls from more than twenty years of writing tracks in the background while other people’s records took priority, and that accumulated time shows in how confidently unshowy this record is. This leans techno and IDM more than anything experimental, dancefloor-facing and beat-heavy across the whole tracklist. The title track builds itself up layer by layer into a pulsating beat while TV dialogue keeps pulling focus sideways, a small disruption that never fully resolves. Nothing here is trying to be difficult, and nothing here needed to be. “R$W” and “Osmosis” are the two that stick hardest. Different rhythms, same underlying intent—Krainik chasing something gritty and repetitive at once, loops that don’t evolve so much as they insist on themselves. Baby Ford‘s influence is audible in how minimal and slightly off-center the drum programming stays, that same stripped tension where less becomes the entire point rather than a limitation working against the track. “Murderer’s Row” leans into that same lineage even more directly, carrying an unintended tribute to Throbbing Gristle in its haze and darkness, deliberately murky where the rest of the EP stays brighter. It’s dance music built by someone who spent twenty years listening to other people make dance music, which sounds like it should produce something derivative and instead produces something oddly assured. He knows exactly which two or three elements a track actually needs and refuses to add a fourth just because he can.   Two EPs, two very different sounds :: Radius Etc‘s Alive & Thriving sits nowhere near that world. This is instrumental hip-hop pushed somewhere stranger, call it hip-hop IDM for lack of a cleaner label, though the term undersells how much dub techno and straight experimental electronic music bleeds into the beats underneath. Norwood recorded this across a blur of hostels, planes, and temporary housing between 2021 and 2025, and the press notes frame it explicitly as documentation of moving from housing instability and food scarcity into something closer to self-actualization. A travel document, in his own words, proof of surviving into thriving. That context sits underneath the music without ever being spelled out inside the tracks themselves, which is the right call. The record doesn’t lecture you about where it came from. It just carries the weight of it. “Goldenlocks” is the standout, and it’s also the most straightforwardly hip-hop beat on the record, except the tempo keeps breaking and the snares reverse and catch themselves mid-hit like the whole beat is tripping over its own feet on purpose. There’s a video for it, one of three the label produced for this release. Little vocal samples surface throughout, adding texture without ever becoming a hook. “Stuttering Spaces (PoplockJam)” goes fully electro, upbeat in a way nothing else on the record quite matches, the most purely fun three minutes here. “One 4 Larry Heard Pt. 1” is the only track running a straight 4/4 kick and it’s catchy specifically because it doesn’t try to be clever about it, same DNA as everything surrounding it just aimed squarely at a dancefloor instead of a headspace. The “Pt. 1” leaves you wondering if there’s a Pt. 2 coming or if the numbering is its own quiet joke about unfinished business. “Go Inside/Outside” is the most abstract piece on the record, a loop cycling endlessly through filters and phasers and pitch shifts like a revolving door that never fully closes, always mid-swing. The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other. They just happen to share a home. If these two EPs are the tone-setters for what Consumers wants to be in its second life, the label picked back up somewhere considerably more interesting than where it left off two decades ago. Drift‘s Manic and Radius Etc‘s Alive & Thriving are both available on The Consumers Research and Development Label. items.body: Analogical Force has long occupied the productive tension between experimentation and the dancefloor’s accumulated memory. Hidden Soul sits firmly within that tension, fluent in its established language and meticulously composed. But perhaps the most exciting possibility lies just beyond that fluency: not abandoning the listener, but trusting them enough to take the familiar somewhere unfamiliar. Muscle memory and accumulated emotional shorthand [AF069] Hidden Soul EP by The 89th Passenger   The 89th Passenger returns to the release schedule of one of contemporary dance music’s more compelling production houses with Hidden Soul, from Paris-based Jeremy Cohen delivering five tidy, DJ-friendly excursions into the familiar architecture of breaks, pads, subs and euphorically melancholic atmospheres. This is music that understands the dancefloor not as a problem requiring reinvention, but as an existing language, complete with its own grammar, muscle memory and accumulated emotional shorthand. “Paper Wings” establishes that grammar almost immediately. Chopped breaks, rounded subs, 303 squiggles and luminous pads are looped into clean, recognisable frames, each element occupying its expected orbit. There is something almost architectural about the neatness of it: familiar components assembled into a functioning environment designed to communicate quickly, cleanly and without obstruction. “Hidden Soul” pushes further into the low end, drawing on break patterns whose familiarity is part of their appeal. Its immediacy is hard to resist; the rhythmic language seems already lodged somewhere in the listener’s body. “What it Takes to Fly” lightens the palette considerably, pairing pretty 303 work with gorgeous tones and gently arpeggiating synths. Its carefully managed peaks, troughs and breakdowns possess an almost cinematic emotional shorthand—the kind of musical optimism that could soundtrack an airplane disappearing into a sunrise. Music interested in making the familiar feel good :: “Eren” continues along those coordinates, allowing textures to breathe while the rhythmic components settle into a quiet, efficient momentum. It feels less like a departure than another room in the same building: different light, familiar construction. “Analog Serenade” finally shifts the pace and texture again, suggesting another route through the material without substantially redrawing its map. And this is where the record becomes more interesting as an artefact of contemporary dance music. Its boundaries are visible. This is not music attempting to make the familiar unstable; it is music interested in making the familiar feel good. The breaks remain breaks, the 303 remains gloriously 303, and the emotional trajectory arrives largely where expectation has already placed it. There is safety here, but it is designed safety: a deliberate perimeter around the possibility of surprise. Yet accessibility and predictability are not the same thing. Music can push its own materials beyond their comfort zone without alienating the listener. In fact, some of the most generous dance music does precisely this, inviting you into a recognisable room before quietly moving the walls. Safety can be useful, but it can also become lazy—an easy creative cheat in which recognition performs the emotional labour that invention might otherwise have to do. Analogical Force has long occupied the productive tension between experimentation and the dancefloor’s accumulated memory. Hidden Soul sits firmly within that tension, fluent in its established language and meticulously composed. But perhaps the most exciting possibility lies just beyond that fluency: not abandoning the listener, but trusting them enough to take the familiar somewhere unfamiliar. Hidden Soul is available on Analogical Force. items.album: Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok :: The Sky Was Out of Tune (Morr Music)
items.excerpt: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together.
items.body: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together. Chkheidze is a Georgian composer and producer based in the Netherlands. Lippok is Berlin, To Rococo Rot, Raster Noton, installation work, decades of treating electronic sound as material that gets layered, cut, reshaped, and left partially unresolved. They met in Tbilisi in 2019 through a workshop program, worked together on Glacier Music II, then built that into Uncontrollable Thoughts, their first joint album for Morr Music in 2025. Morr Music has spent decades in that specific space between electronica, ambient, post-rock, and minimal composition—múm, The Notwist, B. Fleischmann, music where texture and atmosphere carry as much weight as conventional structure. A natural home for this collaboration. The Sky Was Out of Tune pushes further. Eight pieces, titled only with Roman numerals, and they really don’t function as separate tracks so much as sections of one continuous object. That makes sense, the music grew out of a live performance at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie. Everything feels connected by residue. A texture disappears and something remains behind it. A rhythmic idea dissolves into ambience. A metallic sound becomes the thing guiding the next section without announcing itself as such. “I” opens with what sounds like field recording, natural ambience, small bell-like tones, rattling, paper movement, objects handled close to a microphone. Hard to identify exactly what some of those sounds are. Records that begin this way can immediately position themselves as documentary field recording works where the environment becomes the subject. Here the material behaves differently. It’s preparation. Those sounds establish a physical space before synthetic material gets pushed into it. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface :: That becomes one of the strongest ideas running through the record. Chkheidze and Lippok are extremely good at preparing the listener for something before revealing what it is. Ambience gathers density. Distortion arrives gradually. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface before becoming clearer. Metallic sounds enter and disappear like objects moving through the stereo field. No obvious drops. No resolutions. They build toward changes in texture instead, which is a harder thing to make feel earned. Their process on Uncontrollable Thoughts involved long improvisations, selecting ideas afterward, sending projects between one another. Chkheidze contributing drums, piano, vocals. Lippok adding noise, harmony, sometimes reshaping the entire piece. He’s described his production as primarily layering, constructing, collaging, not sitting at a keyboard writing chord progressions. You can hear that philosophy all over this record. Compared to Uncontrollable Thoughts, The Sky Was Out of Tune is more dissolved. The previous album still had recognizable individual pieces—”Bird Song,” “Rainbow Road,” soft beats, organ drones, clear rhythmic personalities moving between tracks. Boundaries here have almost completely disappeared. Uncontrollable Thoughts felt like two musicians improvising compositions. This feels like those same two musicians improvising an environment. The rhythm is still present but behaves more like weather than percussion. Digital texture and ambience overlapping :: Soft electro rhythms surface throughout, especially when the album settles into its more defined sections. Nothing becomes overly forceful. Even when distortion enters it feels incorporated into the ambience rather than placed over it. There are moments that recall the softer edges of early Mille Plateaux material, digital texture and ambience overlapping until it becomes difficult to decide which one you’re actually listening to. The late 90s and early 2000s electronica sensibility is present throughout, that specific understanding that small rhythmic gestures can carry enormous emotional weight if given room. “VII” is the most interesting section on the record and it lasts 35 seconds. The glitches become more exposed, textures start colliding, and suddenly the album sounds like it might move somewhere completely different—like a corrupted transitional file that accidentally became part of the release. Its short duration is what gives it impact. “VII” functions as a doorway into “VIII” rather than a standalone piece. An introduction to the outro. And that tiny moment reveals something about the whole record, Chkheidze and Lippok are comfortable letting an idea exist only as long as it needs to. A texture doesn’t have to develop into a full track. A rhythmic pattern can appear for seconds and disappear. Something can sound important and still never return. The title describes the music unusually well. A sky being out of tune doesn’t mean the environment has collapsed, it means something familiar has shifted slightly enough that you start paying closer attention. That’s what happens here. Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. The Sky Was Out of Tune is available on Morr Music. items.body: Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. An accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation landscape 07 by fields we found / quiet details   Fields We Found is the alias of British musician, mastering engineer and visual artist Alex Gold, who founded the quiet details label in 2023. Following releases on Home Normal, Seil Records, handstitched*, and Ambientologist, Gold has increasingly focused his work on extended listening. The Landscape series grew out of compositions created for his personal meditation practice; over time, the creative process itself also became a form of meditation. Landscape 07, the seventh installment in the series, runs for more than twenty-five minutes. It is an extended live performance constructed from electronic instruments, tape and successive layers of sound. The piece begins almost without a threshold. A broad sound emerges from the haze, already inhabited by tremors, gentle fluctuations and distant trails. During the opening minutes, the music gains weight; the volume rises calmly and glimmers of light move across its surface. From here, Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. “Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined.” ~Mirco Salvadori The presence of tape can be felt in the sound’s internal movement. The notes have porous edges, slight instabilities and a warmth far removed from artificial stillness. Even when everything appears motionless, something continues to shift. The overall balance gradually changes, brighter colours surface and the mass of sound seems to lift. Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined. Gold handles duration with patience and restraint. Each event is allowed to remain long enough to alter our perception of everything around it. In its central section, the piece takes on a darker, more introspective colour. Threads and reflections continue to move through the texture; through headphones, they reveal small lateral movements, like currents. Light then returns gradually and the music expands without losing its composure. This leads to the point of greatest emotional intensity, reached through patient accumulation. The journey feels natural, almost as though it had formed by itself, while retaining the freedom of a gesture made in the moment. The piece asks for a simple kind of openness: to remain, to listen, to give each nuance time to reveal itself and to accept that the inner landscape may change alongside the sonic one. In these passages, distant echoes of German electronic music from the early 1970s begin to surface. The more abstract expanses of Tangerine Dream’s Zeit, the cosmic materiality of early Klaus Schulze and some of Cluster’s suspended atmospheres come to mind in the way timbre becomes form. Fields We Found keeps everything on an intimate, tactile scale. The connection lies in the trust placed in machines, in their natural drift and in the time a sound needs to reveal its hidden folds. Recording the performance directly to tape preserves the element of risk that gives life to such a gradual process. “A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception.” ~Mirco Salvadori An even closer affinity leads to Éliane Radigue. Landscape 07 shares the French composer’s attentiveness to what can emerge from within a prolonged sound and to the variations that appear when the ear stops searching for a melody. The historical and poetic distance remains clear; the surface here is denser and more explicitly ambient. Yet the kind of listening it requires is close to Radigue’s: focused, patient and ready to recognise an event within apparent stillness. Pauline Oliveros’ Deep Listening also comes to mind, particularly in its understanding of attention as an active part of the work, as does Suzanne Ciani, in the gentle way electronic sound can suggest physical movement. Towards the end, the piece begins to subtract. The pressure recedes, its lines grow sparse and what remains reveals its irregularities more clearly. The farewell becomes fragile. The long fade avoids any emphatic sense of closure. A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception. It is an ending fully consistent with the work as a whole: the ear is left to measure the disappearance, while the silence that follows seems to last a little longer. Landscape 07 succeeds because its calmness contains tension. Meditation here has density, pressure and material memory. The instruments breathe, the tapes impart instability and depth, and the studio work preserves the spontaneity of the performance. With each new listen, the hierarchy of details changes: something that first seemed marginal becomes a guide, a fluctuation turns into rhythm, a blur acquires definition. This is music that entrusts its richness to time and draws its strength from time in return. A remarkable entry in the series, and perhaps its most accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation. Landscape 07 is available on quiet details. items.body: A mesmerizing collision of ambient, jazz, electronics and ritualistic textures, this album unfolds like a deep-space journey that never loses its human pulse. Trumpet drifts through electronic vastness Fade In Brighter Age by Pulsar + Demetrio Cecchitelli   Mahorka has a busy schedule and quite an enormous back catalog, covering various electronic music, from ambient to dub, noise and radically experimental. Confirmed sound artists meet new promising ones in the course of indie, challenging music with no regard for major commercial tendencies. I’ve never heard of Pulsar (Leonardo Pucci) before, but I must say he perfectly teams up with Demitrio Cecchitelli. I’m more familiar with the work of Cecchitelli, notably with the sumptuous Empetus (published years ago by Midira). The addition of trumpet player Jacopo Buda to the soundscapes gives an enriched musical meaning to the album, playing the card of instrumental ambient music with partly experimental-jazzy tones and expansive improvs which evolve on dynamic electronic textures. What we can listen to here is nothing less than a furiously enthralling and original musical trip which starts masterfully with the ethno-ritual and spaced-out “Cosmic Dream”. Such a gorgeous piece with its perpetual circular rhythms covered by inspiring and gently minimal trumpet melodic shifts. It is meticulously crafted without being purely ambient, as it conjugates a vast array of influences, from Buddhist-Zen musical attributes to early minimalism and atmospheric, then bassy, chilled-out vibes. It suggests immensity and nature-like vastness, with its colorful timbres resonating in divine harmony. It is a sprawling track with a magnificent development, always suspenseful, melodically ethereal and dynamic. The second track (“Expanding Light”) also operates a nice syncretism and musical dialogue between acoustic ingredients, wind instruments and electronics, but here we enter a more downtempo, softly moving ambience, less lyrical and tripped-out but equally good and perfectly elaborated. The title track (“Fade in Brighter Age”) almost provides a softly moving dream-pop quality, built on guitars, vibrant chords and slowly enveloping wind sequences, largely embracing a lonesome path and a feeling of consciousness at night. All in all, a varied and semi-jazzy atmospheric ambient album with a flowing cinematic edge. Absolutely recommended and easily one of my personal favorites of this year. For fans of John Hassell, Harold Budd, Peter Knight, Loscil, Bersanin Quartett, Nala Sinephro, and Floating Points. Fade In Brighter Age is available on Mahorka. items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — Echorec featured in Prog magazine 106 (February 2020) in an article titled 16 bands to watch this year, before their debut album The Island had even been released. Currently based in Bath, the trio easily deserve a place in that list because The Island is an incredibly mature offering. They even had the audacity to attempt, and successfully pull off a subtle interpretation of the end section of Pink Floyd's Echoes during the 17 minute long closing track The Lamb Returns ? Pink Floyd, listed as 'an artist we also like', being one of the leading exponents of the Binson Echorec analogue delay effect which provided the young band with their name. Made up of Julian Kirk (vocals, guitars and keyboards), Brad McGinty (bass, vocals) and Jake Aubrey (drums and percussion), there's no compromise in the quality or quantity of either lead instrument; Kirk is a genuine multi-instrumentalist who can play stately Gilmour-like guitar but also does an admirable impersonation of Tony Banks playing a fluid ARP solo on The Cinema Show. Despite being momentarily reminded of David Surkamp on Safe at Home (the epigrammatic opener The Water is a piano instrumental) I declined to look for comparisons with Kirk's vocal style because his voice simply seems to fit well with the music. McGinty and Aubrey are also both very capable musicians, meting out inventive rhythm patterns during staccato riffing or bubbling and bouncing along in the melodic sections - this is the essence of the music, it's primarily melodic, it's not derivative, it has plenty of changes and uses a broad palette to produce a nicely-balanced modern prog sound with classic touches.The Island is a concept album that relates the story of a teenage girl's journey of self-discovery. Raised on a lighthouse rock by a single mother who is reluctant to grant her any freedom, she flees to the Island in search of her father. The truth is finally revealed in the epic The Lamb Returns, that her nuclear family fell apart following the early death of her older brother. It's hard to believe that the story isn't personal ? it's well constructed with suitable imagery of yearning, hope, doubt and resolution ? and it's certainly a bold move on a debut release.It's not really a big issue because the entire work is thoroughly commendable, but I don't think the lyrics, which work fine as part of individual song structures and as an overarching narrative, fully rise to the challenge of telling such difficult themes.Stuck in the middle of a pandemic, a streaming-only release is not unreasonable, though getting noticed in a vast industry geared towards rewarding established acts and/or instant gratification isn't going to be easy for a new band with a debut album. In my opinion, the interest generated by exposure through Prog magazine should be maximised by investing in a physical product to be ready for the merchandise stand when gigs resume. I'm pretty sure that Echorec's music will be greeted favourably by the prog community.Three and a half stars

items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — I was given the opportunity to review Jordan Rudess' WIRED FOR MADNESS before I'd ever listened to a note played by Dream Theater and equally shocking, I always used to skip over articles about the band in magazines and books. One good thing is that I was able to approach this review, for the keyboard player's fifteenth solo outing, without any idea of what the music would be like, although it's obvious that I've harboured preconceptions about the band he's most associated with. Another thing on the plus side, I know that Rudess is admired by musician friends whose opinions I respect, one of which lent Rudess his Kurzweil K2600 keyboard for a couple of performances organised by the Italian Dreamers during a Rudess family holiday in Italy around the time of Feeding the Wheel. The K2600 still bears Rudess' autograph. The album cover design neatly encapsulates the story behind the title track, an individual who accedes to becoming partially computerised and as his human self is reduced, he undergoes a procedure to upgrade his mental and physical capabilities. As a result he becomes increasingly separated from the outside world with his computerised portion performing the majority of his routine functions, allowing his mind to travel freely between madness and spiritual enlightenment. In a nod to previous prog epics, the track is split into two parts with a total running time of over 34 minutes and maintains a high tempo throughout. Without any Dream Theater reference points I have struggled to draw comparisons but in terms of wild, creative conceptuality and sheer musical density it comes close to Patrick Moraz's Story of i. It could easily have been dreamt up in 1974 and serves as a tribute to the 70's progressive rock keyboard players who influenced Rudess, Rick Wakeman, Keith Emerson and Patrick Moraz included. Having never heard his playing before I had no idea how good Rudess was, with elegant rhapsodic piano, authentic Hammond organ tones, and sinuous synthesizer runs. The modern sounding keyboards remind me of Eddie Jobson's work on the debut UK album and, when the rhythm section gets into a modern-jazz mood, like Dave Stewart on National Health's swansong DS al coda. I'm not a huge fan of the lyrics but they serve the composition well and, delivered by Rudess himself (apart from guest female vocals from Marjana Semkina in the role of an angel, and Dream Theater frontman James LaBrie at the climactic end to part 2), they are well sung. The track is heavy at times but there are sufficient strong melodies and tonal variation, almost all played at a frantic pace, to keep the listener interested. It goes without saying that his guest musicians are all of the highest calibre. With Wired for Madness parts 1 and 2 taking up more than half of the album and close enough to being able to fill a single traditional LP on their own, the remaining tracks run the risk of acting as filler, though this isn't really the case. Off the Ground is a straightforward pleasant, mellow, reflective piece, a welcome respite from the onslaught that's just taken place, but Drop Twist once again picks up the pace following an early arcade game-like intro. It may not be prog as we know it but the short instrumental allows Rudess to show his chops. Perpetual Shrine could almost be Drop Twist part 2, but if anything it's busier and funkier. It wouldn't sound out of place if it was used as the theme music for an 80s TV detective series based somewhere in Florida... The one track that feels to me to be there to make up the numbers is Just Can't Win. I'm being unfair because I'm not a fan of the Blues, but it performs a similar function to ELP's Tiger in a Spotlight, a moment of relief from the technical bombast but still a little self-indulgent. Here Rudess utilises the guitar talents of Joe Bonamassa and incorporates a full brass section; as a blues-rock song it can't be denied that it pushes all the appropriate buttons. Just for Today is another reflective, slow-paced number but it includes sweeping cinematic strokes before it gives way to the jazzy Why I Dream where the vocal phrasing reminds me of Supersister or Jeff Berlin on Gradually Going Tornado. Wired for Madness showcases Rudess' excellent playing and I believe he's pulled off something spectacular with the 34 minute title-track, an excess to rival anything from the 70s. It wasn't nearly as heavy as I'd feared but covers the whole gamut of prog and prog-related styles, with melody, rather than riff taking the lead. Furthermore, the pacy compositions that bookend the recording makes it sound as though the whole writing, playing and recording was fun. Three and a half stars

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Throughout his career, Jon Anderson has not limited himself to the paths of progressive rock. His constant exploration of diverse musical languages - in search of new textures and nuances and free from conventional constraints - has led him to expand his sonic palette and reflect it in musical works of very different natures. "The More You Know" (1998), his twelfth studio album, is one of those works that strays furthest from the genre that made Yes one of its leading standard-bearers.Prioritizing gentle, melodic structures over any display of instrumental virtuosity, "The More You Know" moves, almost effortlessly, through pop and world music sounds, in which the arrangements and programming form the foundation upon which much of the album rests. Songs like "Magic Love," "Say Jocky," and "Take, Take, Take" are easy on the ears but don't seem to offer anything substantial. On the other hand, when the English singer's more spiritual side comes to the fore, some of the album's best moments emerge, including the melancholic "Heaven's Love" and "Sad," and the jubilant "Youth" with its ethnic overtones.Also noteworthy are the arrangements on "Dancing Fool" and the light soul-jazz of "Free (Some Would Say)," underpinned by the deep, expressive bass of Bobby Jocky, brother of Francis Jocky, who contributes on keyboards and as a composer. The rest of the album hovers in an accessible average that never quite takes off, with the standout feature being Anderson's angelic voice, which is in fine form. That's no small thing, but it's not enough to overcome a production that, at times, feels overly polished.2/2.5 stars

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Finnish band Von Hertzen Brothers released their fifth studio album 'Nine Lives' in 2013 throughUniversal, having previously caught the attention of the press with the records 'Love Remains theSame' and 'Stars Aligned'. This quintet plays an interesting crossover of pop, prog, and folk,offering an eclectic yet accessible type of rock music that definitely has commercial potential butdoes not shy away from unconventional arrangements. The album 'Nine Lives' in particular issubjected to a high-energy, buzzing start, in the face of melodic numbers like 'Insomniac' and'Flowers and Rust', while its ending resorts to mellower, more atmospheric tones that are exploredon the longer songs 'World Without' and 'Prospect for Escape'. Certain instrumental sections are waytoo loud in the recording, especially in the faster tracks in the beginning, but I think thisproblem is taken care of in the second half of the recording. The vocals are fine, but some of thelyrics feel corny, while the album itself strikes you as almost too eclectic, which is probably whatVHB had wanted to do, but this aspect of it may disengage some listeners. I think the main issuewith 'Nine Lives' is the fact that there are very few highlights present. The record is quite solidoverall and the variety of styles covered provides for an engaging listen, but the songs featured onit are mostly hit or miss.

items.body: Darkmechanic released the album “Hypercontrol” on 2 October 2026 through the Slovak label Aliens Production. The eight-track record is the industrial electronic project’s second album and its first release for the label. Alexander Borsov, who records as Darkmechanic, wrote, produced and mastered all eight tracks. “Hypercontrol” comprises: The deceitful idol Puppet Gloomy lake Cau the night cult Hypercontrol Go all….F Resolving a controversy Halloween (Bonus track) Aliens Production describes the album as “a mechanical colossus of industrial energy and electronic flashes.” “Hypercontrol” is available as a digital album on Bandcamp. Aliens Production is a Slovak dark electronics label operating since 1997. Side-Line has previously covered Aliens Production releases by the Polish electro/EBM act Fractal, including “Antidote” in 2023 and “Hide in the light” in 2026, both on the same label. Hypercontrol by Darkmechanic About Darkmechanic Darkmechanic is the solo industrial electronic project of Alexander Borsov, who also records as Dark The Keeper and Stellar Dynamics. The project’s first recorded appearance was a track on the compilation “Dark Virus X-Mas”, released by Russian Dark Community in 2020. Darkmechanic’s debut album, “Ghost Reflection”, followed in 2021, also through Russian Dark Community. Between albums, Borsov contributed remixes to other artists’ releases: “Blood For Blood Remixes” (2023) on DSBP, “Monolith” (2023) by Reagent, “Mvrtyr” (2024) by G.G.F.H. and “Lost EP” (2025) by Synaptic Defect. Darkmechanic also appeared on the compilation “Cyclone Front: Movements and Currents” in 2025. “Hypercontrol”, released on 2 October 2026, is Darkmechanic’s second album and the project’s first release through Aliens Production, five years after “Ghost Reflection”.

items.body: Cry DOPE, a dark electro-pop duo from Tokyo, released its debut digital single “Dark Dopamine” on October 2, 2026. The duo, Syuri and Sonar, sing in both Japanese and English across the track’s 3:03 running time. An official music video followed on YouTube on October 3. The track’s chorus alternates “Han-bun, han-bun, han-bun-bun” (“half, half, half-half”) in Japanese with the English line “Half of me is still asleep.” Each verse plays out as a short back-and-forth: an unfamiliar key in the mailbox, a letter on the fridge that reads only “sorry,” and questions about a name, the time, and whether to go home. The music is as far as we can gather AI assisted or generated. “Dark Dopamine” streams on Spotify, Apple Music and other platforms. About Cry DOPE Cry DOPE is the Tokyo-based duo of Syuri and Sonar. The band describes its sound as music that “sits somewhere between a late-night room and the city outside,” sung in both Japanese and English. “Dark Dopamine,” released October 2, 2026, is the duo’s debut single.

items.body: Magic Wands released the single “Guardians” on October 2, 2026 through Metropolis Records. The Los Angeles dream-pop duo of vocalists and guitarists Dexy and Chris Valentine describe the track as a look back at a period that no longer feels real: “This is a song about looking back on a time in your life that doesn’t feel real anymore, even though it really happened.” “Guardians” is the second track lifted from “Sun Kiss,” a new Magic Wands album due in early 2027. It follows “Diamond Rain”, issued in mid-August, which was the first single from the same record. Guardians by Magic Wands “Guardians” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp. Magic Wands’ 2026 singles and EPs “Guardians” and “Diamond Rain” extend a run of releases that started with “Cascades,” the album Magic Wands issued on October 24, 2025. The duo opened 2026 with “Sacred Mirrors,” a January collaboration with Psychedelic Furs guitarist John Ashton. The six-track “Wishing Well” EP followed in April, and Side-Line reviewed it that August. A six-track “Remixes” EP reworking songs from “Cascades” followed in June. Magic Wands remixed Peter Murphy’s “Swoon” in late spring, and Side-Line covered that single when Peter Murphy released “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix)” on May 29, 2026. About Magic Wands Magic Wands formed in Nashville, Tennessee, in the summer of 2008 around vocalists and guitarists Dexy Valentine and Chris Valentine, who began writing together after Dexy moved from Los Angeles to Nashville. The duo later relocated to Los Angeles, where they are now based. Their sound blends dream-pop with shoegaze, post-punk and goth textures, carried by layered guitars, droning synths and Dexy’s vocals. The band debuted with the album “Aloha Moon” (Bright Antenna, 2012), preceded by the EP “Magic Love & Dreams” (2009). “Jupiter” followed on Cleopatra Records in 2016, and “Abrakadabra” on Etxe Records & Productions / Casa del Puente Discos in 2018. Magic Wands self-released “Illuminate” in 2020, then signed to Metropolis Records for “Switch,” released May 12, 2023. Side-Line reviewed “Switch” that September, having already covered the duo’s single “Fortune” in April 2022, the single “Time” that May, and the remix album and tour announced that August. Magic Wands’ sixth album, “Cascades,” arrived in October 2025 and set off the run of singles, remixes and EPs that continued through 2026. “Guardians” now carries that chronology into “Sun Kiss,” the duo’s next album, scheduled for early 2027.
